CINCINNATI (AP) — El zurdo de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, Blake Snell, abandonó su apertura la noche del miércoles contra los Rojos de Cincinnati después de una entrada debido a rigidez en la ingle izquierda.
“Me sentí bien todo el día (y luego) en el penúltimo lanzamiento del bullpen, (sentí) un tirón”, dijo Snell. “Hice un lanzamiento más, luego corrí hacia el dugout. Estuve como hablándome a mí mismo durante toda esa primera entrada. Iba a intentar llegar a cinco, pero realmente no tenía muchas posibilidades de hacerlo”.
Snell permitió un sencillo a Sal Stewart y ponchó a un bateador en la primera entrada. Stewart fue sorprendido fuera de base para terminar la entrada. Snell realizó 19 lanzamientos, 10 en zona de strike antes de abandonar el juego.
Snell (4-1, 1.86 de efectividad) comenzó la temporada en la lista de lesionados por una inflamación en el hombro izquierdo. Se sometió a una cirugía en mayo para retirar cuerpos sueltos y espolones óseos del codo izquierdo.
Ha tenido problemas en la ingle en el pasado. En 2021, pasó tiempo en la lista de lesionados por una distensión del aductor izquierdo, se perdió casi un mes en 2022 y tuvo una estadía en la lista de lesionados en 2024 debido a distensiones en la ingle .
“No se siente tan grave como las veces que hemos lidiado con esto en el pasado”, dijo Snell. “Seguí lanzando en dos de ellas y me distendí ambas. Así que para mí parar, eso es una primera vez” .
Snell dijo que le gustaría tener una apertura más en la temporada regular.
“Obviamente, contento de que nos lo avisara temprano para sacarlo del juego, no empeorarlo”, dijo el mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts. “Creo que lo primero es que veremos cómo amanece mañana, cómo se siente, darle más tratamiento. Cuando regresemos a LA entonces podemos tomar esa decisión”.
Los Dodgers utilizaron seis relevistas después de que Snell salió en la derrota 6-2 ante los Rojos que les impidió asegurar el título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional. Ya aseguraron su 14ta clasificación consecutiva a la postemporada.

Blake Snell exits Dodgers’ loss early because of injury
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — The trouble started as Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell threw in the Great American Ball Park bullpen before the game.
“I felt good all day, and then the second-to-last pitch of the bullpen, I threw a slider and then I felt it grab,” Snell said of the groin tightness that ended up taking him out of the Dodgers’ 6-2 loss to the Reds early. “So I was like, ‘Alright, let’s see what we can do.’”
With Snell guiding the ball without driving hard off his back leg, his velocity was down a tick or two through a 19-pitch first inning. He gave up one hit, a single to Sal Stewart, which he quickly erased with a successful pick-off that caught Stewart in an inning-ending run-down.
“I was going to try to get through five [innings],” he said, “but I just knew I didn’t really have a good shot at doing that and remaining healthy.”
In a conversation with manager Dave Roberts, pitching coach Mark Prior and head athletic trainer Thomas Albert, they all agreed the best course of action would be to pull Snell from the game. Right-handed reliever Blake Treinen replaced him in the second inning.
With only 10 games left in the season, it’s unclear when Snell will be ready to pitch again.
“The next couple days are really going to decide,” Snell said. “But I’d love to throw on my next [scheduled start day]. Either there or a couple days after. But definitely, I want to try to get one more in the regular season.”
Teoscar Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday in the Dodgers’ win against the Reds was his second home run in as many nights.
The Dodgers’ loss marked Snell’s eighth start of the season. His 2026 debut was delayed by shoulder fatigue. And then after one start, he landed back on the injured list to undergo arthroscopic surgery to remove loose bodies from his left elbow.
Since returning, he hasn’t given up more than one run in a start. Through Wednesday, Snell has a 1.86 ERA. And he’s a key member of the Dodgers’ projected postseason rotation.
“I don’t think anyone can sit here right now and say what’s going to happen in the next week to 10 days,” Roberts said, noting that the team would decide whether to send him to get imaging after they returned to Los Angeles. “It’s under the, ‘I’m glad it’s not worse and we caught it early’ [category].”
Snell has a history of left groin and adductor strains. He spent time on the IL in 2021, 2022 and 2024 for such injuries. He said this injury didn’t feel nearly as severe as any of those.
“[In the past] I felt like that and then I kept pitching on two of them and strained both of them,” he said. “One was a grade one, one was a grade two. So I’m definitely happy I stopped. … I’m aware if I kept pitching, I definitely would’ve strained it. So for me to stop, that’s a first. Maybe I’m growing up. I don’t know. But that was definitely the right move. And next couple days, we’ll see where we’re at and go from there. But I think I’ll be good to go.”
The last couple years, in an effort to avoid another groin strain, Snell has incorporated Copenhagen planks into his routine, strengthening the area.
“I thought I had this thing figured out,” Snell said. “Well, technically, I still do. I didn’t strain it, so that was a good thing. … I haven’t felt it at all until that pitch in the bullpen, and I was just kind of thrown off by it. So I’ve done what I’ve needed to do to be strong and healthy. Definitely a shock to me.”
After Snell left the game, the Dodgers used six relievers to get through seven innings. They combined to give up six runs and 12 hits, including a pair of home runs.
Left-hander Kris Bubic, acquired at the trade deadline while on the IL (flexor strain, shoulder impingement), made his Dodgers debut in the eighth inning. In his first major-league appearance since mid-May, he allowed an infield single and recorded two strikeouts in a scoreless inning.
The Dodgers missed a chance to clinch the division with a win. And the Padres beat the Rockies on Wednesday to keep the division race mathematically alive.
So, the Dodgers will get another shot at champagne showers in Cincinnati Wednesday when left-hander Justin Wrobleski takes the mound. The Dodgers optioned right-hander Bobby Miller after his 2 ⅓ innings Wednesday and plan to recall righty Landon Knack, Roberts said.
The Dodgers’ pitching plans for the next couple weeks are in flux.
Though right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto and left-hander Tarik Skubal have been rounding into the best versions of themselves down the stretch, Snell’s injury is the latest to deplete the ranks.
Right-hander Roki Sasaki (right middle finger blister) has been on the IL for almost three weeks. He threw a four-inning, 48-pitch live batting practice session Wednesday, with Dermabond covering the sensitive area on his finger.
The Dodgers had planned to discuss how to deploy him when he returns from the IL, but after the game, Roberts said to “make sure guys have ample rest,” his next outing will be a start.
Sasaki would be lined up to pitch against the Padres next week.
“It’s playable,” manager Dave Roberts said of Sasaki’s blister. “And given the Dermabond, the time that he’ll have in between this next outing, the hope is that it’s dang near close to being healed.”
Right-hander Tyler Glasnow hit a rough patch in his last two starts but said his back, which sidelined him for three and a half months, “feels good.” The Dodgers sent him back to Los Angeles after the series in Miami to cut down on the number of flights he’d have to sit on before his scheduled start Friday.
“Get him home, get him acclimated to Pacific Standard Time, not have to do two legs,” Roberts said. “So Tyler feels great. He’ll be ready to go on Friday.”
Roberts reiterated after the game that he’s “not concerned with Tyler,” who came out of a bullpen session Wednesday feeling “normal.”
If the Dodgers need another spot start in the next week and a half, they have right-hander Emmet Sheehan waiting in the wings. They optioned him to triple-A Oklahoma City on Monday, in favor of an extra reliever. But over his last two major-league starts, he’s limited opponents to one run and five hits in 11 ⅔ innings.

CINCINNATI — Now what?
Roki Sasaki threw 48 pitches in four simulated innings to Dodgers hitters on Wednesday afternoon, testing the blister on his right hand that landed him on the injured list. He gave up a home run to Eliezer Alfonzo but otherwise “was good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
Sasaki threw with Dermabond on his injured finger. A surgical adhesive used to close cuts and incisions, pitchers are allowed to use it in games if their team gets permission from MLB in advance.
“He came out of it well,” Roberts said. “So we have to huddle up here and figure out what’s his role. What does it look like as we sit here on the 17th or 18th of September, whatever? So the number one most important thing is that he came out of that session well, and then now we got to figure out how to plug him in. He’s going to be important, but I just don’t know right now what role.”
Sasaki seemed destined for a bullpen role again this postseason, a role he assumed successfully last year. But the Dodgers have reason to hesitate on turning Sasaki into a reliever with Blake Snell leaving his start after just one inning on Wednesday night and Tyler Glasnow’s status.
Glasnow flew back to Los Angeles after his start in Miami. It was the second consecutive start in which Glasnow was not sharp and this time he could be seen in the dugout stretching out his back. But after the game, he said his back felt fine and Roberts said Glasnow threw a “normal” bullpen session in L.A. on Wednesday and is scheduled to make his next start on Friday night.
Sasaki is penciled in now to start during the series against the San Diego Padres in Los Angeles next week and remain a starter at least for now.
“One can argue it’s best to take down a couple starts, keep him built up, because if something does happen, he’s built up,” Roberts said. “The other side is you can assimilate him into the ’pen and get comfortable in that role – if that is the role.
“But again, I don’t want to speak out of turn and say that’s done, because it’s not.”
NO SHO
The Dodgers are about to complete their first road trip in three seasons without Shohei Ohtani. Yoshinobu Yamamoto might have missed Ohtani more than any other of his teammates.
“It’s been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse,” Yamamoto joked through his interpreter when asked about Ohtani’s absence. “All I have is Roki, but he doesn’t really talk to me.”
Back in Los Angeles, Ohtani has been receiving treatment for his knee and bicep injuries. According to Roberts, Ohtani began swinging a bat, hitting off a tee this week.
“There’s going to be a consistent build-up,” Roberts said. “Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Ohtani will be eligible to be activated from the IL next Wednesday. Whether he is ready to play that day or shortly after, Roberts said the expectation is that Ohtani will return in time to play before the regular season ends on Sept. 27.
“I do,” Roberts said. “Whether it happens or not is to be determined. But I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games. Don’t know how many of them.”
COMING/GOING
Right-hander Edwin Diaz made his fifth rehab appearance with Triple-A Oklahoma City on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless inning to close out the Comets’ playoff berth-clinching victory. Diaz did allow a double to a fellow big-leaguer on rehab, Miguel Andujar.
Meanwhile, Edgardo Henriquez returned to Los Angeles and underwent an MRI, which confirmed the diagnosis of a “low-grade back strain,” Roberts said. He won’t be eligible to pitch again in the regular season but Roberts said the Dodgers are “hopeful” he could come back for the postseason.
Left-hander Kris Bubic was activated from the 60-day IL before Wednesday’s game and right-hander Paul Gervase was returned to OKC. In order to clear a spot on the 40-man roster for Bubic, Triple-A outfielder Ryan Ward was designated for assignment.
Right-hander Landon Knack will be added to the active roster before Thursday’s game and Bobby Miller will be returned to OKC.
ALSO
Outfield prospect Charles Davalan (the 41st pick in last year’s draft) was named MVP of the Class-A Midwest League and Great Lakes manager Jair Fernandez was named the league’s Manager of the Year. Davalan hit .292 with 24 home runs and a .937 OPS. He is scheduled to play in the Arizona Fall League, where he is expected to start testing out a possible conversion to second base.
UP NEXT
Dodgers (LHP Justin Wrobleski, 11-5, 3.78 ERA) at Reds (RHP Brady Singer, 6-14, 5.38 ERA), Thursday, 9:40 a.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM

Despite dour predictions from some insiders, Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani might be back in action for the Boys in Blue sooner rather than later.
Ohtani hit off a tee on Tuesday in his bid to return from knee, arm and neck pain, issues that led to a very uncharacteristic slump in the weeks before he was placed on the injured list.
Having already been shut down as a pitcher, Ohtani has also been sidelined as a hitter, though that may not be for too much longer.
Dave Roberts shares expectations for Ohtani’s return
On Tuesday, manager Dave Roberts said Ohtani “felt good” after hitting off the tee.
“I don’t know what’s in store for tomorrow, but I know there’s going to be a consistent buildup. Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive and hopefully, we can just keep building towards that,” he said.
When asked if he expects Ohtani back during the regular season, Roberts answered with a definitive “I do.”
View this post on Instagram
“Whether it happens or not is to be determined, but I do expect him to be back to play in some regular season games,” he said. “Don’t know how many though.”
Roberts’ prediction flies in the face of at least one Dodgers insider, who predicted that the Japanese superstar was out for the rest of 2026.
The saga has also raised questions about whether Ohtani was honest with the team about his injuries, and whether the team perhaps mismanaged their superstar.
Many of those questions will only be answered with time, though if Ohtani does indeed come back this year and looks more like his old self, the criticism will likely be much quieter.
What would Shohei Ohtani’s return mean for the Dodgers?
While Ohtani’s absence hasn’t impacted the Dodgers too much this month, that could be because the Boys in Blue have one of the easier September scheduled in the National League.
In October, though, the playoffs are on, and the quality of opponent will be much higher.
Some of those likely opponents, such as the Atlanta Braves, have recently given the Dodgers fits, and a healthier Ohtani returning to the batting order would almost assuredly improve the Dodgers’ chances of winning a third straight World Series.
Ohtani’s replacement, the much-hyped prospect Josue De Paula, has flashed moments of brilliance in his first few games in the big leagues, but getting back perhaps the best baseball player ever would be a huge boost for the Dodgers, especially from a mental perspective.
Do you think Shohei Ohtani will be back this year and, if so, will it be before the playoffs begin?

item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani’s aching right arm. Freddie Freeman’s throbbing right knee. Edwin Díaz’s disastrous form on a minor-league rehabilitation assignment.
Whatever problems surfaced in recent weeks, the Dodgers were able to convince themselves they could overcome them.
The reason: Even with Ohtani unable to pitch, they had the most talented starting rotation of this era.
Suddenly, that source of comfort is a major concern.
Blake Snell departed his start in Cincinnati on Wednesday after just one inning with what was described as a tight left groin.
Consider that Tyler Glasnow traveled directly home from Miami rather than to follow the Dodgers to Great American Ball Park for their four-game series against the Reds, and there are reasons to be worried.
Very worried.
With an inconsistent offense and combustible bullpen, the Dodgers were going to be heavily dependent on their starting pitching in the playoffs.
That rotation could now be unraveling.

The last time Snell strained his left groin was when he was pitching for the San Francisco Giants in 2024. He was sidelined for a month.
For what it’s worth, Snell is convinced this particular injury isn’t severe and plans to make his next start, according to people familiar with this situation.
“Stopped before it got too bad,” one of the people said.
Then again, weren’t similar claims once made about Ohtani?
As for Glasnow, he remains on track to pitch on Friday.
Manager Dave Roberts said Glasnow skipped the Cincinnati leg of the trip to better prepare for his starting assignment at Dodger Stadium against the San Francisco Giants.
“Get him acclimated to Pacific Standard Time,” Roberts said.
By sending Glasnow back to Los Angeles, the Dodgers spared him a three-hour flight from Miami to Cincinnati.
Glasnow was sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, and Roberts intimated something could be wrong with him after his most recent start. In his last two appearances, the 6-foot-8 right-hander gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings.
The questions about Snell’s and Glasnow’s health came at a time when the rotation was coming together before the postseason.
Snell in particular was sharp after returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months. Before his early departure on Wednesday, Snell was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average since he was activated from the injured list on Aug. 11.
Snell wasn’t the only Cy Young Award-caliber pitcher rounding into shape.
The day before Snell scaled the mound, it was Yamamoto’s turn to do so, and last year’s World Series Most Valuable Player pitched seven scoreless innings in a 4-0 win over the Reds.
The seven-inning start was the third in a row for Yamamoto, who improved his record to 14-8 and lowered his earned-run average to 2.51.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
The opening game of the series was started by Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was acquired from the Detroit Tigers before the trade deadline.
Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Just last week, the Dodgers had a playoff rotation that would have looked to other teams like the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
Now, there’s a chance they could be forced to send Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan to the mound in playoff games.
The Dodgers could conceivably win a championship with a rotation of Yamamoto, Skubal, Sasaki and Sheehan but that would require their offense to be productive.
How much can the Dodgers count on that, considering the physical problems Ohtani and Freeman have encountered? And how would using Sasaki as a starter instead of a reliever affect their bullpen?
Snell removed himself from his start on Wednesday so the Dodgers wouldn’t have to find out. The question is whether he did so in time. Their season depends on it.

La irregularidad de Edwin Díaz abre la puerta a que Dodgers evalúe dejarlo fuera del roster para los playoffs.
La presión crece alrededor de Edwin Díaz en un momento especialmente delicado para los Dodgers. El relevista boricua llegó a Los Ángeles con el cartel de cerrador élite y con un contrato de tres años y $69 millones de dólares, una inversión diseñada para reforzar el último inning de un bullpen que había dejado dudas durante 2025. Sin embargo, su primera temporada en Dodger Stadium se ha alejado de ese plan.
Díaz ha tenido problemas para encontrar consistencia, salud y comando. En 16 apariciones con los Dodgers registra una efectividad de 11.85, con 18 carreras limpias permitidas en 13 innings y dos tercios, además de cuatro salvamentos desperdiciados en 11 oportunidades. En 2025, todavía con los Mets, había firmado una efectividad de 1.63 y solo había dejado escapar tres rescates en 31 oportunidades.
El panorama se volvió aún más complejo después de su última aparición en Grandes Ligas, el 17 de agosto ante los Rockies de Colorado. Díaz permitió tres carreras en un inning, con cuatro hits recibidos, y al día siguiente ingresó a la lista de lesionados por inflamación en el cuello. Ahora continúa en Triple-A con los Oklahoma City Comets, donde busca recuperar ritmo, ajustar su mecánica y convencer al club de que puede aportar en la recta final.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Edwin Díaz tuvo una salida perfecta en el triunfo agónico de los Dodgers sobre los Royals
Edwin Díaz enfrenta una presión inesperada con Dodgers
El foco está en su lugar dentro del bullpen y, más concretamente, en la posibilidad de que no llegue a ocupar nuevamente el noveno inning ni entre al roster de postemporada.
Para un pitcher de su trayectoria, la situación resulta poco habitual. Díaz fue uno de los relevistas más cotizados del último mercado de agentes libres y los Dodgers lo firmaron para aportar experiencia, ponches y seguridad en los juegos cerrados. Su llegada respondía a una necesidad clara del equipo, que buscaba una figura estable para cerrar los partidos de alto voltaje.
Los resultados, no obstante, han obligado a Los Ángeles a manejar el caso con cautela. Su recta ha perdido velocidad en comparación con temporadas anteriores y su ángulo de brazo bajó de un promedio de 19 grados en 2025 a 15 grados durante esta campaña. Esa modificación ha afectado tanto su ubicación como la efectividad de sus pitcheos, especialmente una recta que ya no genera los mismos swings fallidos.
El problema no se limita a los números. Díaz pasó cerca de tres meses fuera tras someterse a una cirugía artroscópica para retirarle cuerpos libres del codo derecho. Volvió a finales de julio, pero apenas pudo disputar algunos juegos antes de que la inflamación en el cuello lo enviara de regreso a la lista de lesionados.
Los Dodgers evalúan el roster de playoffs
De acuerdo con Ken Rosenthal, no sería descabellado que los Dodgers excluyan a Díaz de su roster de postemporada, incluso con el peso de su contrato. El razonamiento dentro de la organización sería simple, aunque duro para un relevista de su estatus. En octubre, Los Ángeles necesita llevar a sus mejores brazos disponibles, no necesariamente a los de mayor salario o trayectoria.
Dave Roberts también reconoció públicamente que Díaz necesita mostrar señales claras antes de recuperar un sitio asegurado. El manager mantiene confianza en el talento del puertorriqueño, pero ha dejado claro que el equipo necesita evidencia de que puede competir en situaciones de alta exigencia. Esa frase resume el momento del cerrador, que ya no tiene el puesto garantizado por historial ni por contrato.
La decisión tampoco se explica únicamente por la irregularidad de Díaz. Los Dodgers cuentan con alternativas en el bullpen y Tanner Scott ha asumido buena parte de las oportunidades de salvamento durante la ausencia del boricua. Scott ha convertido 21 de 24 chances de rescate y se ha establecido como la opción más frecuente para el noveno episodio.
Además,la organización ha sumado profundidad con el zurdo Kris Bubic, adquirido en la fecha límite de cambios. Bubic viene de una sólida rehabilitación, con cinco innings y dos tercios sin carreras y nueve ponches, una incorporación que amplía las variantes de Roberts para octubre.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Dodgers se desploman en Arizona: suman siete derrotas consecutivas
Oklahoma City será una prueba decisiva
La estadía de Díaz con los Oklahoma City Comets no es un trámite. Cada salida en Triple-A tiene valor en su intento por regresar a las Grandes Ligas. Aunque tuvo actuaciones sin carreras en sus primeras apariciones de rehabilitación, su presentación más reciente encendió las alarmas al permitir cinco carreras, dos hits y tres boletos en apenas dos tercios de inning.
El desafío para Díaz pasa por recuperar el comando y confianza en su repertorio. La velocidad de su recta ha rondado las 96 millas por hora, una cifra que sigue siendo competitiva, pero menor a sus estándares. En Triple-A también se ha visto una búsqueda mecánica para elevar el ángulo de su brazo y devolverle mayor vida a sus lanzamientos.
Los Dodgers no necesitan que Díaz vuelva de inmediato a la función de cerrador. Su ruta más lógica sería regresar en apariciones de menor presión, acumular innings efectivos y demostrar que puede ser una opción fiable. El contrato de $69 millones de dólares no garantiza un lugar cuando el equipo se prepara para la etapa más importante del año.

Dodgers news: Roki Sasaki presents good playoff problem for Dave Roberts appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
After being pulled from the Los Angeles Dodgers' rotation after suffering a blister on his throwing hand, Roki Sasaki has been working his way back to full strength.
Scheduled to throw a four-inning simulated live session on Wednesday instead of a normal start against the Cincinnati Reds, The California Post's Jack Harris reported that Sasaki performed well, to the point where Dave Roberts and company will have to have discussions about how best to use the second-year flame thrower when the postseason rolls around.
"Roki Sasaki's four-inning/48-pitch live session today went well, per Dave Roberts," Harris wrote. "The team is gonna huddle up now and decide if he will return as a starter or reliever. His likely playoff role is in 'pen, but he's also their best rotation insurance in case of any late injuries too."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
On one hand, Sasaki proved in 2025 that he can be a really good option out of the bullpen, where he finished multiple games for the Dodgers as a closer last October. With Edgardo Henriquez placed on IL as he tries to get healthy enough to make the playoff roster, the Dodgers really don't have an elite right-handed arm in their bullpen and could use one situationally alongside stalwart arms like Alex Vesia, Jack Dreyer, and Tanner Scott.
And yet, as LA fans know all too well, things can change in a hurry, and if injuries start stacking up once more, keeping Sasaki ready to go long might not be the worst idea either, just in case.

Los Angeles Dodgers left-handed pitcher Blake Snell has exited Wednesday's game against the Cincinnati Reds after one inning in a concerning development with less than two weeks to go in the regular season.
Snell pitched a scoreless first inning with one strikeout across 19 pitches. There didn't appear to be anything noticeably wrong with him during the frame, but his fastball velocity was down.
At the conclusion of the first inning, Snell went down to the clubhouse alongside team trainer Thomas Albert.
Now, he's out of the game, with right-hander Blake Treinen replacing him in the bottom of the second inning.
What is Blake Snell's Injury?
The Dodgers announced Snell was removed from the game with left groin tightness.
Manager Dave Roberts will provide a more substantial update after the game, which will include whether or not Snell will need to go on the injured list.
Dodgers Can't Afford a Blake Snell Injury Right Now
Snell opened the year on the IL as he recovered from shoulder inflammation that dated back to last year. He returned for one start in May before going right back on the IL to undergo surgery to remove loose bodies in his elbow.
He missed another three months before returning in August, and has been absolutely dominant ever since.
Entering Wednesday, Snell was 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA in six starts since coming off the IL. Including Wednesday's scoreless first inning, he has 47 strikeouts over 35.2 innings and hasn't allowed a home run in that stretch.
The Dodgers are relying on Snell and fellow superstar pitchers Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal to carry them in October. Thus, the team will hope Snell isn't dealing with anything serious moving forward.
Who Will Replace Blake Snell in Dodgers Rotation if He's Forced to Miss Time?
The Dodgers' starting rotation is dealing with an onslaught of injury concerns as the season winds down.
While the rotation is led by Yamamoto and Skubal (who underwent midseason elbow surgery while with the Detroit Tigers), behind them is a bunch of question marks.
Tyler Glasnow has struggled since returning from a nearly four-month absence due to a back injury. Justin Wrobleski has been removed from the rotation amid his forearm injury and struggles. Roki Sasaki is currently on the IL with a blister. Eric Lauer is out for the season due to an elbow injury.
Then there's Shohei Ohtani, who won't return as a pitcher this year (and may not even be 100% as a hitter).
The Dodgers recently demoted Emmet Sheehan, but could recall him if Snell goes on the IL. He was sharp over his two September starts, allowing one run over 11.2 innings.
If Snell isn't forced to miss time, the Dodgers will take a big sigh of relief knowing their superstar trio in the starting rotation is intact with October looming. If he's forced to go on the IL, though, it will be yet another massive blow in the team's chances to three-peat.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to capture a sweep over the Cincinnati Reds this week.
LA has opened up a few-game lead over the Atlanta Braves for the No. 2 seed in the NL, and the Dodgers can clinch the NL West on Wednesday. Their pitching staff looks as dominant as it ever has, with all arms looking fully healthy… except for Roki Sasaki.
Sasaki, who has been out since the Dodgers’ series with the Braves last month, took a big step in his potential return to MLB on Wednesday during the Reds series.

Roki Sasaki got a blister on his finger during his last start against the Braves, which landed him on the IL.
If Dodgers fans remember correctly from last season, Roki Sasaki was one of the team’s highest-leverage bullpen arms throughout their World Series run.
LA has other arms they may go to this October, but perhaps Roki Sasaki is a pitcher who rises to the occasion in the biggest moments, which the Dodgers would like to utilize if possible.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edwin Diaz responded to manager Dave Roberts’ postseason warning with a better outing.
Roberts was asked Monday about Diaz’s concerning Triple-A performance. He has a 12.46 ERA over 4.1 innings in his current rehab assignment due to neck inflammation.
The manager didn’t mince words about Diaz’s postseason status.
“He needs to pitch better. I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But it’s like, where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well,” Roberts said.
Diaz’s most concerning outing came on Sunday, when he allowed two hits, three walks, and hit a batter, allowing a total of five runs.
On Wednesday, Diaz came out to the challenge Roberts posed to improve his final line and delivered a promising outing.
He allowed one hit, a 100+ mph double, according to Baseball Savant, along with two flyouts and a groundout.
Diaz had no whiffs, which is certainly concerning for a pitcher known for swing-and-miss stuff.
On the bright side, Diaz averaged 1.6 MPH more on his fastball, and he had more induced vertical break on the slider, adding another two inches from his season average.
Where does Edwin Diaz go from here?
The OKC Comets have four games left on their schedule, meaning Diaz could make two more appearances before he needs to return to the Dodgers for additional action.
At that point, Diaz will get some chances to show the Dodgers why he should be on the playoff roster.
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” Roberts said.
“So my bet is that he will be (on the roster). But again, there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us, again, to sort of bet on. And so my bet is yes, but we still got to see something.”
Diaz’s reputation can take him far and give him the nod in a bullpen with some other question marks, but it will ultimately come down to his final outings for the Dodgers.

item.content:encoded:
Edgardo Henriquez’s regular season was already effectively over once the Dodgers placed the hard-throwing pitcher on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort.
Henriquez, whose 103.6-mph fastball was the fastest pitch thrown by a Dodger since at least 2008, was diagnoesed with a low back strain. Bill Plunkett of the Southern California News Group reported Wednesday, Sept. 16, that the pitcher is “hopeful” he can return in October after getting the results of an MRI exam.
“Hopeful” and “probable” can be a world apart. In Henriquez’s case, it’s unclear whether his hope stems from the severity of his diagnosis, or from his faith that the Dodgers will play deep enough into the postseason to give him a chance to recover.
In either event, the Dodgers’ bullpen without Henriquez is a very different one than what they hoped to carry in their quest to three-peat as World Series champions.
Henriquez’s fastball touched 103.6 on June 2 in a game against the Arizona Diamondbacks, and again on Aug. 29 in a game against the Detroit Tigers.
Speed is just one facet of Henriquez’s game. His 71-to-25 strikeout-to-walk ratio, combined with only 37 hits allowed in 60 innings, gave the right-hander an at-times untouchable arsenal.
No right-handed pitcher had made more appearances for the Dodgers this season than Henriquez’s 61. Without him, manager Dave Roberts might have to get creative.
Right-hander Roki Sasaki, a starter during the regular season and a reliever during the team’s 2025 World Series run, might return in a relief role once he’s recovered from a finger blister. Edwin Diaz, who is currently on a rehab assignment of his own, struggled mightily in the closer’s role this season — but might be needed in some capacity just to get the Dodgers through to the end of the postseason.
Diaz, a three-time All-Star, had an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances with the Dodgers before landing on the injured list with a neck injury Aug. 16.

Los Angeles Dodgers key reliever Edgardo Henriquez got the official diagnosis for his lower-body injury that has him on the injured list.
Henriquez has a "low-grade" back strain, and the team is "hopeful" he'll be back for the postseason, manager Dave Roberts said.
Roberts described the MRI results as "positive," which should be a relief for fans hoping to get their best bullpen arm back in time for the playoffs.
The Dodgers placed him on the 15-day injured list, meaning that he is not eligible to return until September 29th, effectively ending his regular season.
All eyes will be on Henriquez as we look toward October, when he is expected to be a high-leverage arm, possibly even the closer if he is able to get back to pitching again soon.
Why Henriquez is so important for the Dodgers
Henriquez has a 2.62 ERA, with a 2.50 FIP. He misses the barrel of the bat, strikes out hitters, and limits home runs like one of the best relievers.
He throws triple digits, which may explain his back issue, but the pitch's movement and growing command make it a deadly weapon out of the bullpen.
While he lacks the high-leverage experience of players like Edwin Diaz and Tanner Scott, Henriquez carries himself confidently and exudes a strong presence whenever he takes the mound.
It is unclear how quickly the Dodgers will pull the trigger on Henriquez in the playoffs for a high-leverage role, but given what he has proven this year, they will try to lean on him as much as his health permits.

The Los Angeles Dodgers will be without relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez for the remainder of the regular season. The 24-year-old was placed on the 15-day injured list on Sept. 14.
Henriquez’s injury was initially labeled as lower back discomfort. With further imaging and testing, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the injury is a “low-grade back strain,” per MLB.com’s Sonja Chen.
Although Edgardo Henriquez’s regular season is over, he still remains someone that Los Angeles can get back for the postseason. Dave Roberts said that he remains “hopeful” that Henriquez can return in October.
Edgardo Henriquez’s Dominant 2026 Season
Coming off limited MLB experience, Edgardo Henriquez displayed the best pitching of his career in 2026. The high-velocity right-handed pitcher was a reliable piece of the Dodgers’ bullpen throughout the season.
In 61 appearances, Henriquez finished with a 4-1 record, 2.85 ERA, and 1.03 WHIP across 60.0 innings pitched. He also added 11 holds and two saves in the season.
Henriquez was among the hardest-throwing pitchers in the league. The 24-year-old’s fastball reached as fast as 104 miles per hour this season.
“He hit 103 mph or higher 17 times, more than any Major League pitcher not named Jacob Misiorowski (140 pitches) or Mason Miller (33 pitches). But Henriquez became more than just a hard thrower this year, developing the command and the confidence to be a leverage weapon for the Dodgers,” MLB.com’s Sonja Chen wrote.
Dodgers Still Searching For Answers on Edwin Diaz’s Status
The Los Angeles Dodgers made closer Edwin Diaz the most expensive reliever in MLB last offseason, signing him to a three-year, $69 million contract.
Diaz’s first season with the Dodgers has not been what many expected. While dealing with injuries, Diaz’s season stats include a 2-2 record, 11.85 ERA, and 2.56 WHIP across 13.2 innings pitched.
While dealing with inflammation in his neck, Edwin Diaz has remained on the injured list since Aug. 18. He has since begun a rehab assignment, with results that haven’t gone well.
The 32-year-old allowed five runs in a rehab appearance in Triple-A Oklahoma City on Sept. 13. Dave Roberts says that if Diaz’s game doesn’t improve, he could be left off the Dodgers’ postseason roster, according to The Athletic’s Fabian Ardaya.
“He needs to pitch better,” Roberts also mentioned. “I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But it’s like, where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that.”
Diaz made another rehab appearance on Wednesday, pitching one scoreless inning. However, he didn’t produce a swing-and-miss and gave up a double, says Ardaya.

The Los Angeles Dodgers moved closer to restoring their pitching depth before Wednesday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
Right-handed starter Roki Sasaki threw a live batting practice session at Great American Ball Park in Cincinnati. Dodgers management is hoping the session clears the last hurdle in Sasaki’s recovery from a right middle-finger blister that has sidelined him since the end of August.
A return to the active roster appears imminent, though the Dodgers haven’t decided whether he’ll resume his rotation spot or shift to the bullpen for the final weeks of the regular season.
Either way, Sasaki is expected to work exclusively out of the bullpen once the playoffs begin.
Sasaki could give manager Dave Roberts’ pitching staff a boost as the Dodgers gear up for October.
Before landing on the injured list, Sasaki posted a 4.60 ERA and 1.33 WHIP with 117 strikeouts over 119.1 innings across 23 starts. He was pulled from his Aug. 26 outing against the Atlanta Braves once the blister appeared. With a fastball averaging 97.8 mph and a plus splitter, Sasaki carries real swing-and-miss upside.
Bullpen an option
Should the Dodgers use him in the bullpen down the stretch, his triple-digit fastball and put-away splitter could bolster L.A.’s late-inning group immediately. Returning him to the rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell would instead add starter depth and help manage workloads over the final two weeks of the regular season.
Keeping Sasaki’s finger healthy is a priority for the Dodgers front office, and avoiding another setback matters as the 24-year-old works his way back. Despite his inconsistent season, Sasaki has shown great stuff and figures to be a key piece of L.A.’s pitching staff as the postseason nears.
A clean live BP outing could lead to a short rehab assignment or a quicker activation before the Dodgers face the San Francisco Giants in their next series. Whether he lands in the rotation or the bullpen for the stretch run, the Dodgers will have another weapon at their disposal heading into October.

- As October approaches, injuries and recoveries are poised to reshape the MLB postseason picture, with nearly every contender juggling critical absences and fragile returns.
- Houston shuts down Carlos Correa after an ankle setback, the Yankees finally get Max Fried and Aaron Judge back, while Shohei Ohtani looms as the Dodgers’ biggest question.
Carlos Correa is out. Max Fried is back. Shohei Ohtani is somewhere in-between. And questions linger over the postseason availability of several other MLB difference-makers as October approaches.
Here is a look at the injury status and hopeful returns of impact players on playoff qualifiers and contenders:
American League East
Tampa Bay Rays: Acquired from Baltimore at the trade deadline, swingman Tyler Wells posted a 1.50 earned-run-average before right forearm tightness sidelined him. He is back solely pitching from the bullpen, and could be a key piece for the Rays in their surprising surge to the division title.
Hopeful return: Slick-fielding shortstop Taylor Walls is recovering from a right hip flexor strain and signs point to him returning by October.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
New York Yankees: The return of staff ace Fried is huge for a team that has clinched a wild-card berth and remains a long step behind the Rays for a division title and first-round bye. The left-hander out of Studio City Harvard-Westlake High gave up one run while walking none over seven innings in his longest start in almost five months. Fried has had two arduous IL stints dealing with a bone bruise on his left elbow.
Hopeful returns: Giancarlo Stanton or Trent Grisham returning in October would give the Yankees lineup additional pop. Three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge has been back for a week since missing more than three months with a fractured rib.
Boston Red Sox: A right quadriceps strain has kept All-Star center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela sidelined for two weeks. However, Rafaela told NESN that he expects to be activated this weekend, a substantial addition to a team that likely will play the Yankees in wild-card series.
Hopeful return: A year ago, Garrett Crochet was 18-5 and led the AL with 205 1/3 innings pitched. This year, left shoulder inflammation and a lat strain have kept him sidelined since April. However, he has ramped up bullpen sessions and is targeting a postseason return as a reliever.
American League Central
Chicago White Sox: The most improved team in baseball is desperately trying to hold off the Guardians and win a division title after finishing last two years in a row. Chicago has enjoyed good health and added journeyman outfielder Tommy Pham from the Phillies on Aug. 31. Pham was activated from the IL on Wednesday and could provide valuable postseason experience to complement his young new teammates — he has hit .315 in 37 career playoff games.
Hopeful return: Drew Thorpe was reinstated from the 60-day IL on Wednesday and is an intriguing option. The right-hander from Cal Poly SLO was a key piece in the 2024 trade that sent Dylan Cease to the Padres but has spent nearly two full seasons on the shelf. Now healthy, his inclusion on the playoff roster would be a gamble that his elite stuff can mask his inexperience.
Cleveland Guardians: Jo Adell didn’t come off the IL, but the addition of the former confounding Angels prospect in an August salary dump has bolstered the Guardians’ outfield — long a problem area. Adell has driven in 28 runs in 38 games with Cleveland and joins glittering rookie Chase DeLauter and steady veteran Steven Kwan in a productive outfield.
Hopeful return: Reliever Shawn Armstrong, who signed a one-year, $5.5 million contract last offseason, has been sidelined since July 24 with a calf strain. Barring a setback in his final minor league rehab appearance, he could be activated in time for the playoffs.
American League West
Houston Astros: Correa, whose second act with Houston has been a flop because of injuries, was working on an accelerated comeback from May ankle surgery. A few days ago team officials expressed optimism, but Tuesday they decided to shelve their shortstop when the ankle became inflamed after a workout. Houston is clinging to a one-game lead over the Texas Rangers in the AL West.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note.
Texas Rangers: Still in contention despite spending much of the season under .500, the Rangers welcomed back pitcher Nathan Eovaldi and third baseman Josh Jung from the injured list over the weekend. A calf strain had kept Jung sidelined since July 21 and Eovaldi had been out since Aug. 7 with elbow inflammation. Eovaldi, who has started in all but 20 of his 339 MLB appearances, will pitch out of the bullpen.
Hopeful return: Nothing of note
National League East
Atlanta Braves: Reynaldo López inflated hopes of a late-career surge when he posted a 1.99 ERA over 25 starts in his first season with Atlanta. But injuries — including right shoulder inflammation this season — have severely limited his contribution. López was placed on the IL again Tuesday.
Hopeful return: Bryce Elder had an arthroscopic procedure to clean up bone fragments in his right knee on Sept. 8. The hope is that the right-handed starter can recover quickly enough to be counted upon in the postseason.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.
Philadelphia Phillies: Although an MRI found no structural damage to the throwing shoulder of stalwart starter Jesús Luzardo, the left-hander remains a question for the playoffs. He was placed on the 15-day IL retroactive to Sept. 12, and it is doubtful he could pitch again in the regular season. Luzardo has a 2.87 ERA across 29 starts this season.
Hopeful return: Tanner Banks, a major contributor to the Philadelphia bullpen in 2025, was reinstated from the 60-day IL over the weekend. Although he wasn’t effective earlier this season, Banks is welcomed back because Phillies relievers have been poor against left-handed hitters.
National League Central
Milwaukee Brewers: Huntington Beach Marina High product Jake Bauers has suffered from shin splints almost all season, and the pain has kept him from playing the outfield lately. He can play first base, but that takes slugger Andrew Vaughn out of the lineup. Bauers, with 26 home runs and 83 RBIs, has been a key bat for Milwaukee. He has been particularly tough against the Dodgers, batting .348 with a .483 on-base percentage.
Hopeful return: Brandon Woodruff, one of the best starters in baseball when healthy, is rehabbing from shoulder inflammation that sidelined him in July. The Brewers are nearly guaranteed a first-round bye, giving Woodruff an extra week to build stamina.
Chicago Cubs: Shortstop and team leader Dansby Swanson will be welcomed back after missing a month with a left oblique injury. He is expected to rejoin the Cubs during their weekend series against the Cincinnati Reds.
Hopeful return: Left-handed starter Justin Steele is progressing through bullpen sessions and is almost ready to take the mound after missing the entire season with a left elbow flexor strain. Steele, whose record was 16-5 in 2023, likely would pitch from the bullpen in the postseason.
National League West
Dodgers: The loss of center fielder Andy Pages is significant. He can bat near the top or bottom of the order, displays power and speed, and had improved his patience at the plate enough to earn a career-high 45 walks in 128 games.
Hopeful return: Getting Ohtani healthy enough to produce at the plate is a priority, and his absence from the mound shouldn’t be felt if Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow pitch to their capabilities. Meanwhile, Edwin Diaz might not even make the playoff roster.
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
San Diego Padres: While recovering from Tommy John surgery, starter Joe Musgrove made it a goal to be ready for the postseason. Recovery difficulties between starts have made his status doubtful, however. Nick Pivetta, on the other hand, has pitched well in two starts since coming off the IL and appears ready.
Hopeful return: Ramón Laurenano, a 2025 trade deadline acquisition with a potent bat, last played May 30 because of hip inflammation. However, he told reporters that the chances of him playing in the postseason are “less than 5%.”
Arizona Diamondbacks: Zac Gallen was activated from the 60-day IL and Michael Soroka from the 15-day IL, giving the D-Backs two starters in their push to win a wild-card berth. Gallen, a proven starter who has been horrendous in 2026, has been out since the All-Star break with elbow inflammation. Soroka was out only two weeks with the same ailment.
Hopeful return: Third baseman Nolan Arenado suffered an injury to his left thumb Tuesday, the same injury he sustained in late August. It’s doubtful the injury would sideline the 14-year veteran with games this week being so important, yet the Diamondbacks have to hope the injury doesn’t impact his productivity.

item.content:encoded:
Teoscar Hernández Is Delivering When The Dodgers Need Him The Most
LOS ANGELES — During a months-long spiral at the plate, Teoscar Hernández tried to maintain his upbeat, convivial persona.
But for much of the summer, before his September revival, it was difficult for the Dodgers’ fun-loving, seed-tossing veteran presence to look or feel like himself.
"I try to stay positive and bring the same energy that you guys know and see everyday — smiling, making jokes," Hernández told me. "But at the same time, it’s really hard."
(Photo by David Jordan/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts noticed his typically jovial outfielder looking a bit more sullen at times, too. It was understandable.
Hernández, a fixture in the Dodgers’ lineup whose clutch hitting, encouraging nature and penchant for performing on the sport’s biggest stage helped his team win back-to-back World Series titles, had a respectable .785 OPS when he went on the injured list on May 29 with a left hamstring strain.
But the 33-year-old did not look the same when he returned a month later. From June 29 to Aug. 29, his .592 OPS was the ninth-lowest mark among all qualified MLB hitters over that stretch.
"Some of the joy was sucked out," Roberts told me, "because it’s hard to be so joyful when you’re not performing. He was still a good teammate, always a good teammate, but I know there were a lot of frustrating moments for him."
Hernández’s struggles were compounded by the fact that the Dodgers were also getting little from their other corner outfielder, Kyle Tucker, or the rest of an offense that looked lifeless for much of the summer.
But now, at a crucial juncture for his team with All-Stars Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages sidelined, another All-Star in Freddie Freeman battling knee soreness and the playoffs just weeks away, Hernández is taking his frustration out constructively.
He is annihilating the baseball in September, leaving his summer slump behind and giving the Dodgers reason to believe in the depth of their offense again.
"When he catches fire," Dodgers infielder Tommy Edman said, "he’s as good as anybody in the game."
Even among Hernández’s best career stretches, the tear he’s on now stands out. Every part of his offensive profile is enhanced.
Hernández, who’s prone to swing and miss even when he’s going right, is making better swing decisions. From last month to this month, he has lowered his chase rate from 36.7% to 24.8%, tripled his walk rate from 4.3% to 15.1% and cut his strikeout rate nearly in half from 31.2% to 18.9%.
And along with a more selective approach, he is punishing every mistake in a way he couldn’t earlier this season.
Hernández’s hard-hit rate has skyrocketed from 34.5% in July to 47.5% in August to 60% this month. His average exit velocity this September (96.6 mph) is the highest of any month in his career.
Eight of his 10 hardest-hit balls this season have come in the last two weeks, and his power is being generated by the highest average bat speed he has produced in any month over the last two seasons (74.1 mph).
It’s a far cry from where Hernández was just a couple of weeks ago, when his year-long struggle against right-handers had the Dodgers considering using a platoon in left field. That no longer appears to be a consideration.
"Right now," Roberts said, "it’s just night and day."
So how, exactly, did Hernández find his way back?
"The most important part, he’s healthy," Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas told me. "If he’s healthy, we can see the Teo that’s running hard on the bases, stealing bases, going first to third. Obviously the bat is there because it’s his best tool, but seeing the complete player now is really refreshing."
Earlier this season, Hernández’s downturn looked familiar.
A year ago, he had the highest batting average on the team when he went on the IL in May with an adductor strain. He returned two weeks later, then watched his OPS precipitously drop 200 points from May 21 (.927) to July 21 (.727).
Clearly, the lower-body injury had lingered, throwing off his swing and sapping his power.
This year, it was happening again, only with his hamstring. The swing that worked for him before the injury was putting too much pressure on his lower half. Upon his return from the IL, he had a .562 OPS overall in July and a team-worst .496 OPS against right-handed pitching in August.
"I told Dave, ‘If you feel like you have to use somebody else in there, just do it,’" Hernández said.
(Photo by Meg Oliphant/Getty Images)
That would not be necessary. At least, not again after Aug. 25. The decision to sit him that day was noteworthy, considering the Dodgers were coming off an off day and facing a Braves team they were battling for a first-round bye.
In hindsight, it might have served as a wake-up call.
On Aug. 26, Hernández returned to the lineup in Atlanta with a two-hit day. He then ended the Dodgers’ next series in Detroit with a two-run homer off Framber Valdez, which might have been the turning point.
"I think that at-bat gave him the extra life that he needed for the last part of the season," Rojas said. "Obviously, baseball is about confidence, and you find confidence with success, and I thought that’s what he needed. He needed, like, one good swing that he knows he’s back, and then all of a sudden we see the results we get now."
There’s also a mechanical component to Hernández’s upswing.
Too often, Hernández felt both rushed and late at the plate as he worked his way back from his hamstring injury. He has since opened his stance in an effort, he says, to slow his body up, prevent his front hip from flying open and give him more time to see the ball. He has also traded his more subtle toe tap for a slightly more exaggerated leg lift and hip twist as a timing mechanism that seems to be producing more power.
These were moves he used before in his career. Now healthy, he feels his body can withstand the added force once again.
Sometimes with hitting, the littlest tweaks can yield the biggest results.
"That’s why it’s hard," Hernández told me. "One day, you don’t know what you’re doing. The next day, you change barely — sometimes it’s your hands, sometimes it’s your legs, sometimes it’s how low, how tall [in the stance] — and it can click, and you go on a heater."
Even compared to heaters of the past, though, this one is unlike most for Hernández. If September ended today, his 1.211 OPS this month would be the highest mark in any month of his career.
Hernández maintains that his confidence never wavered through the rough patch; that he knew, at some point, things would turn. His teammates shared that belief.
This was the same guy, after all, who homered in every playoff series last season.
(Photo by Melina Pizano/Getty Images)
"The clutch gene and everything that he has in him, the reason why we got him and the reason why we’ve been so good with him in the lineup the last couple years, nothing changed this year just because of a bad stretch," Rojas told me. "To be honest with you, I was never concerned about it … I want nobody in a big at-bat more than Teo."
After the big hit last month in Detroit, Hernández returned home, made the swing changes and provided the elusive clutch hit the scuffling Dodgers’ offense had been missing with a walk-off double to salvage a series against the Cardinals.
That hit helped spark an eight-game winning streak for the Dodgers, who started to look like themselves again.
Their ebullient left fielder is looking that way, too.
"I feel really good right now," Hernández said. "I’ve been working really hard for this, and I’m glad and happy that everything is coming together."

The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to win their series against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday.
The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
On Wednesday, LA has another superstar pitcher on the mound in left-hander Blake Snell.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going [Wednesday] — you feel good about preventing runs,” manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."
Opposite Snell will be left-hander Andrew Abbott, who's 6-11 with a 4.78 ERA and 120 strikeouts over 154.1 innings this season.
He's allowed seven earned runs in two of his last three starts, and has a 7.71 ERA since the start of August.

- Tommy Edman, CF

- Teoscar Hernández, DH

- Kiké Hernández, 3B

Josue De Paula, Max Muncy and Alex Freeland are out of the lineup with the left-handed pitcher on the mound.

item.content:encoded:
gambit – noun
a chess opening in which a player risks one or more pawns or a minor piece to gain an advantage in position
Now, if your mind immediately went to the Marvel Comics character and you were confused, fair enough. Here's the clip you likely thought of, so we can all feel better and get to the heart of the essay.
And for the record, Freddie Freeman is hardly a minor piece, but giving up a major piece for tactical advantage is called a sacrifice, which wouldn't be appropriate given the circumstances here, as Freeman returned to the lineup for the September 15 game against the Cincinnati Reds.
A funny thought occurred to me while watching Freddie Freeman these last few months:
"Where did his power go? He sure seems like he's hitting into more double plays than I remember."
Looking at Freeman's stats for the year, apart from the power and RBI numbers being down a bit, nothing looks amiss. Honestly, I originally dismissed the feeling that something was wrong because Freeman was hitting up a storm for about a month after the All-Star Break.
There wasn't much power behind it, but when someone has a slash line of .367/.402/.411 over 24 games starting from the All-Star Break, pointing out fault feels like searching for a fly in the ointment. Yes, Freeman only had four doubles, eight RBIs, and nearly three times as many strikeouts as walks, but the overall body of work looked pretty good.
Freeman had a solid couple of games in Denver where he hit for doubles power and used the entire field. However, since the Denver series, where Freeman was hitting for average, he's just not.
When you aren't hitting for either average or power, alarm bells tend to finally ring.
Power drained
On September 9, Freeman was kept out of the lineup for right knee soreness and was considered day-to-day. To his credit, Dave Roberts did mention Freeman's slump on September 9.
Roberts said there was no one incident that caused Freeman's knee soreness, but he believes it has impacted his performance at the plate lately.
"Freddie does a really good job of hitting against his front side, and then when you can't do that with your front side, your right knee, then you're compromised," Roberts said. "I see there's a lot more swing-and-miss the last few days. That's just not who he is."
In the 18 games since the Colorado series until the start of play on September 15, Freeman has a slash line of .215/.338/.292. He does have his only home run of the second half, and his strikeouts-to-walk ratio is about 1.5/1 instead of 3/1 earlier in the year.
The problem is more of the eye test: Freeman is starting to finally look, and maybe move, like his age.
The splits on Baseball Savant from last year to now tell a pretty glaring tale: if you want to beat Freeman in 2026, go low and in. Also, Freeman feasted on center-cut pitches last year, not so this year.
I'm not a hitting expert, but having a diminished knee would make it harder to rotate to hit stuff middle in. On the September 13 broadcast of the finale against the Miami Marlins, Dontrelle Willis pointed out how Freeman is compromised rotationally generally, as pitches he would normally drive the other way are being weakly hit.
Even after Freeman hit a career-high and now league-high in double plays on Sunday, the Dodgers are not seriously entertaining putting Freeman on the injured list, per Katie Woo of The Athletic:
"I think it's one of those things where we've got to manage it … just pick spots to give him an off day here or there," Roberts said. "Again, we've just got to make sure he's at optimal health when we finish the season. So I think that he might not love it, but giving him a day off here or there might be beneficial."
The Dodgers don't believe an IL stint is necessary. Instead, Roberts is working in frequent off days. That's rare for Freeman, who hasn't played in fewer than 147 games in any season as a Dodger. Freeman had a scheduled day off over the Dodgers' previous nine-game homestand and also served as the designated hitter twice in that span. He wasn't in the lineup in the last game of the homestand on Wednesday, and following a team travel day, he also sat out Friday's game.
[Emphasis added.]
Freeman insists he feels fine.
Freeman hitting into two double plays and having a key miscue that contributed to the season and series loss to the Miami Marlins seems to indicate otherwise. It's worth noting that Freeman hit another tailor-made ground ball to second on a pitcher's pitch in his final at-bat that likely would have turned into another double play had Mookie Betts not doubled earlier in the frame.
"Just talking to him today, he said he felt good," Roberts said. "Obviously, the swings don't indicate that, don't validate that. On the defense, he's obviously not moving as well as he's used to.
"I think that he's doing anything and everything he can to prepare. But yeah, the last week, it's pretty obvious that he's not himself in the box."
Freeman won't be in Monday's starting lineup, Roberts said, but should play Tuesday…
[Emphasis added.]
Much like the sense one had when watching the Americanized remake of the original 1954 classic Gojira, Godzilla: King of the Monsters, one would expect a sense of deja vu right now, even with character actor Raymond Burr long dead.
Japanese Original, American Remake
I am typically not one to mince words, and I shall not do so here. Along with Dustin Nosler of Dodgers Digest, I was dead on the money regarding the Dodgers' malpractice in not acting decisively on Ohtani and his reluctance to admit injury in the face of personal dogma of success.
I argued that the Dodgers had bungled spectacularly, and events worked themselves out to prove my initial hypothesis correct on all fronts. Now the team has backed itself into a corner regarding Ohtani.
Contrary to what some might think, I did not enjoy being right. Frankly, I am correct often enough that I do not need the constant validation, unless it comes from either the Dodgers broadcast team or national media. (In which case, gimme.)
On September 11, Katie Woo of The Athletic wrote an op-ed recently that pulled few punches:
Nobody is blameless in the Shohei Ohtani injury saga. Not the Los Angeles Dodgers' front office, which should have been more proactive in protecting the team's biggest star. Not Ohtani, who downplayed the severity of his symptoms. And while hindsight is always 20-20, there were warning signs throughout the last few weeks that suggested a stint on the injured list was the safest course of action if the organization wanted to give its prized star the best possible chance at healing in time to begin the Dodgers' quest to win three straight World Series.
As the Dodgers prepare to be without Ohtani until Sept. 23 at the earliest, their biggest concern has become a reality. When Ohtani — who is expected to be placed on the injured list on Friday — does return, there is no guarantee he'll be in optimal condition for the postseason.
[Emphasis added.]
Um, excuse me? To quote one of the finest bits of media from the 2010s, I get to channel Chris Taylor for once and declare the following:
I know, Ms. Woo means nobody relevant, but words matter, and any excuse for referential comedy is a good one.
"I think that if it were a postseason game tomorrow, (Ohtani) would be in the lineup," manager Dave Roberts said Wednesday afternoon, hours before announcing Ohtani would be placed on the IL. "I think that now you're talking about two weeks, 14 days. I feel that that's substantial. He'll be in a much better place than he was today. Is it going to be to 100 percent? Probably not. But I do think that with this time that we're taking now he'll be in an adequate spot to finish the season."
Adequate is a far cry from healthy. It is fair to question how Ohtani was handled in the second half. Should he have attempted a pitching comeback, knowing his physical health was limited? Should the Dodgers have stopped that push sooner, or placed him on the injured list earlier? In their first season of managing Ohtani as a full-season two-way player, there was always going to be some trial and error. That was acknowledged from the start of the season by both Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman. And in fairness, there was a cognizant effort to keep Ohtani as rested as possible, including a season-long six-man rotation and an attempt to maneuver Ohtani's starts to line up on games prior to a team off day, when possible.
Hindsight is generally 20/20. I am sure if the Dodgers were armed with foreknowledge in a do-over, they would not have Ohtani's best pitching starts of the year be in Houston and San Francisco … in May.
At the risk of retreading previously covered ground, we shall conclude this portion with Roberts' regret, especially considering that Ohtani tweaked his arm in his last played game and did not immediately tell anyone about it:
Looking back, it is something Roberts wish happened a week ago.
"I think if we look right now, here today, I would love to go back and put him on the IL," the manager said. "But I did feel at that moment in time, we all felt that giving him four days was sufficient. He was agreeable. Getting him out there on Monday with the hope that he would be able to play tonight. But where we're at right now, sure."
The Dodgers should have followed their own advice or learned from their handling of Ohtani to send Freeman back to Los Angeles for ten days before arriving in Cincinnati.
They didn't.
The Dodgers have calculated that whatever value Freeman can generate in the waning days of the season is greater than the potential benefit of having Freeman recuperate for ten days, having three days against the already-eliminated San Francisco Giants to use as a tune-up. Hence, the title of this essay: the Freeman Gambit.
Yesterday's game showed promise, even with a couple of moments that made one grimace. Freeman talked about how his three-hit performance likely ensured he would play on September 16.
Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic reported Roberts' comments on the health issues of players like Ohtani, Freeman, and Edgardo Henriquez after the Dodgers clinched their fourteenth consecutive postseason appearance:
"I think right now it's front of mind, it's not great," Roberts said. "But I will say this: Once you get to October, athletes have a magical way of feeling better. It happens every single year, where there's that extra adrenaline that athletes get when you get to the postseason."
The Dodgers still boast what is likely baseball's most talented roster and an established track record of postseason success that might be enough to make history. That was the heart of Roberts' toast: that the Dodgers have not yet played their best baseball.
They still can.
"We just haven't really gotten everyone all synced up at the same time," Muncy said. "So it is a scary thought to think what we could possibly do if we did that. So hopefully that's still ahead for us at the right time."
Whether the Freeman Gambit pays off over the next two weeks before the upcoming postseason tournament is an open question. Gambits are risky, even when they work.

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series.
Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen.
There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers.
Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball.
No player influences the outcome of a game as much as a starting pitcher, and the Dodgers are the only team that will be able to roll out one Cy Young Award-caliber arm after another after another.
The Dodgers were negligent with Ohtani, and the verdict on their management of Freeman is pending, but they at least set up their pitchers the right way.
The rotation is more than a collection of big names. In Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, the Dodgers have three starters who are peaking in time to deliver the kinds of performances that will be required for them to win their third consecutive World Series.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched seven shutout innings on Tuesday in a 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, marking his third consecutive seven-inning start.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
Yamamoto isn’t alone.
The day before Yamamoto’s start, Tarik Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Blake Snell, who is scheduled to take his turn in the rotation on Wednesday, was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average in the six games he started since returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months.
The one source of concern in the rotation is Tyler Glasnow, who, like Snell, was slow-played in his return from an injury. Sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, Glasnow showed promise in his first couple of starts after he came back. But in his last two starts, he gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings. But as the team’s No. 4 starter, he is unlikely to start more than one game in any postseason series.
Even before Ohtani was placed on the injured list because of right arm and left knee injuries, the starting pitching was likely going to have to carry the Dodgers – much as it did last year.
Recent developments have shifted even more of the burden to the starting pitchers.
Edwin Diaz, their $69-million closer, was blow-torched for five runs in ⅔ of an inning in the most recent game of his minor-league rehabilitation assignment. At this point, he’s a longshot to make the postseason roster.
Diaz’s failure to rediscover his All-Star form will have major ramifications on the bullpen, which lost ninth-inning candidate Edgardo Henriquez to a lower-back problem for the remainder of the regular season. Henriquez’s status for the playoffs remains a mystery.
Manager Dave Roberts’ current ninth-inning choice, Tanner Scott, is in a minor slump, as he has given up runs in five of his last 12 apperances.
While the Dodgers will have to find a closer – Roki Sasaki? – their ability to create favorable matchups in the innings before the ninth is also under question. The simplest way to address those uncertainties will be for the starters to pitch deeper into games. Last year, Yamamoto pitched a complete game in the National League Championship Series and another in his next start in the World Series. Snell had an eight-inning start in the NLCS.
The greater problem could be the already-inconsistent offense, which could go into the playoffs with physically-compromised versions of Ohtani and Freeman.
Freeman missed three of five games before starting at first base on Tuesday. Freeman collected three hits in the game, but he’s 37 years old and the Dodgers can’t be certain how his right knee will hold up.
As for Ohtani, Roberts reported on Tuesday that he resumed baseball activities. Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return before the end of the regular season, but hedged his prediction.
“Whether it happens or not,” Roberts said, “is to be determined.”
If the Dodgers don’t know if Ohtani will be able to even step into the batter’s box next week, how could they possibly count on him to be a consistent source of offense?
They can’t.
In other words, the margin for error could be miniscule for the Dodgers. Their starting pitchers might have to be close to perfect. The challenge will be formidable. But considering who will be pitching for them, it will be very much in the realm of possibility.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have allowed Freddie Freeman to play through a right knee injury as of late, while occasionally taking him out of the lineup when they see fit.
The Dodgers took a similar approach with Shohei Ohtani’s various ailments, but the team has been slightly more willing to rest Freeman compared to the four-time MVP.
Given the way Ohtani’s health regressed while continuing to play through injury, it begs the question of whether the Dodgers are making the same mistake with Freeman.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts acknowledged the concern over the weekend, but believes Freeman’s situation is different and does not necessitate a trip to the injured list.
“I think that’s certainly a valid question,” Roberts said on SportsNet LA. “I just think that right now with where we’re at in the season, an IL is not an option in the sense of I personally don’t think we have a better option. So I don’t think it needs to be 10 days, but could it be more than one?
“That’s a fair question. I’ve got to talk to the training staff, Freddie, and ultimately make that decision. But I don’t think an IL makes sense at all.”
Both Roberts and Freeman previously confirmed the knee injury is affecting the 37-year-old at the plate and in the field. The good news is that resting Freeman for just a couple of days has proven to reduce the severity of discomfort.
The Dodgers are not concerned with the injury getting worse, but they will continue to monitor his condition to make sure that remains the case. Before Tuesday’s game, Roberts said he would be watching each of Freeman’s at-bats closely to evaluate his right knee.
Freeman said his knee felt better heading into Tuesday’s contest after missing Monday’s game.
“Feels better today than he did yesterday, which is a good thing. I’ll re-evaluate after tonight,” Roberts began. “But obviously, there’s a day game on Thursday, so just kind of being mindful because I want him in that game on Thursday. I’ll be watching him closely.”
Dodgers need Freddie Freeman down the stretch
The Dodgers still have plenty to play for this season after clinching their 14th consecutive playoff berth.
L.A. is also closing in on another National League West title, but they still have work to do to clinch a top-two seed in the National League. Securing a first-round bye would be significant for the Dodgers, given the current injuries to Ohtani, Freeman and others.
