Mookie Betts and Kiké Hernández wore No. 21 Los Angeles Dodgers jerseys against the Cincinnati Reds on Tuesday night as part of Major League Baseball celebrating Roberto Clemente Day, which is observed every Sept. 15.
MLB permits nominees and previous recipients of the Roberto Clemente Award to wear a No. 21 jersey, and Betts was the winner of last year’s honor. Puerto Rican natives are also allowed to wear the number in honor of Clemente, which Hernández again took advantage of.
Will Smith is the Dodgers’ nominee for this year’s Roberto Clemente Award, and while he did not play in the team’s 4-0 win over the Reds, it also appears he didn’t elect to wear No. 21. Both Betts’ and Hernández’s transaction pages listed them as wearing the number, while Smith’s page still showed him wearing his usual No. 16.
Betts went 0-for-4 with a strikeout against the Reds. Hernández, like Smith, did not appear in the Dodgers’ victory.
The Roberto Clemente Award is presented annually in recognition of the Major League player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.
The concept of honoring Major League players for their philanthropic work was created in 1971 as the “Commissioner’s Award.” The recognition was renamed to the “Roberto Clemente Award” in 1973 as tribute to Clemente following his passing while delivering relief supplies for earthquake victims in Nicaragua on Dec. 31, 1972.
“I was obviously too young to remember Roberto Clemente, but from the people that I respect and what he was as a person, certainly supersedes what he was as a ballplayer, which says a lot,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA.
“Just unfortunately way too young. It’s very cool that young players, current players, understand who Roberto Clemente was and they have that award every year. It’s a big feather in everyone’s cap. Baseball is certainly better with Roberto Clemente.
“I met his family in Pittsburgh, so that was pretty cool. Been to the Roberto Clemente museum in Pittsburgh, which was great for me as well.”
How to vote Will Smith for Roberto Clemente Award
Fans can now vote for the Roberto Clemente Award winner via MLBTogether.com/clementeaward (in both English and Spanish). Fan voting extends through the final day of the regular season on Sunday, Sept. 27. The winner of the fan vote will count as one vote among those cast by the blue-ribbon panel.
The league-wide winner of the Roberto Clemente Award will be honored at the 2026 World Series following selection by the aforementioned panel. It includes representatives from the commissioner’s office, Capital One, MLB-affiliated networks (MLB Network, FOX Sports, ESPN and TBS), MLB.com, National Baseball Hall of Fame, as well as Roberto’s children, Enrique, Luis and Roberto Clemente, Jr.
Smith is looking to become the fifth player in Dodgers franchise history to win the honor. Previous recipients include Betts (2025), Justin Turner (2022), Clayton Kershaw (2012) and Steve Garvey (1981).

Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman has been battling right knee pain, but the worst of it may be behind the team’s contact specialist.
Entering Tuesday’s game, Freeman was on a 3-for-30 cold streak and had missed three of the last six games because of his knee issue.
Things looked shaky for Freeman, who has built a reputation as one of baseball’s most consistent players.
However, he put together his best game in weeks, going 3-for-5 on singles, but showing the elite bat-to-ball skills that make him a candidate to bat around .300 year in, year out.
After the game, manager Dave Roberts noted that Freeman looked more like himself.
“It looked good,” Roberts said. “It looked more like Freddie.”
Freeman had asked Roberts before the game, jokingly, if he could play on Wednesday, a scheduled day off, if he got three hits.
As a result of Freeman’s performance, the manager is allowing Freeman to skip an off-day on Wednesday and play again, with the infielder eager to get the ball rolling.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep,” he said.
“So today was [get the] foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit, and it kind of worked. I wasn’t squaring the ball up in the game, but I’ll take those three hits and keep that work going tomorrow, and hopefully we’ll get hot.”
What does Freeman’s uptick mean for the Dodgers?
With the best rotation in baseball, the Dodgers are left scrounging around for offense any way that they can find it.
Teoscar Hernandez, Josue De Paula, and Mookie Betts have been the most consistent sources, with Max Muncy and Will Smith in the picture as well.
Still, the Dodgers need as many players in a spot as possible to deliver timely hits, and Freeman’s experience and skills make him a clear-cut candidate to step up.
To deliver results quickly, as he manages his knee and struggles, Freeman has made a mechanical change, getting out in front of the ball to catch it earlier on his bat.
The result may be less clean contact and hard hits, but more consistent contact, with the idea that it makes him valuable come the postseason.
“I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable,” he said. “I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
Freeman has the right approach to deliver just what the Dodgers need. The entire offense does not need to be excellent; simply being good enough will lead to a three-peat.

When the Los Angeles Dodgers promoted Josue De Paula to the majors last week, they did so in full knowledge that the 21-year-old had more errors (eight) than assists (six) as a Double-A outfielder.
After playing 58 games in left field and 37 in right field for the Tulsa Drillers, De Paula has spent all but five innings at designated hitter during his first five days in the majors. When he caught the only fly ball hit in his direction over five innings Sunday in Miami, De Paula and the Dodgers could exhale. He got the first one out of the way.
It will be difficult for manager Dave Roberts to take De Paula out of the lineup once Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list if he continues to reach base at such a high clip.
Yet it will be easier to keep De Paula in the lineup if he can play a corner outfield position. To that end, Roberts is hopeful the rookie can become a better defensive outfielder in short order.
"I just think that — just being candid — I don’t think that he’s valued it as much as he will," Roberts said, via Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register. "And it just has to be important. Certainly, when you get to the big leagues, outs are important, converting outs are important.
“I think that he’s a young player. I mean, he’s 21 years old. His bat has certainly got him here, but it’s our job to make him value defense and get him to be a better defender.”
Besides their mandate to make De Paula a more complete baseball player, the Dodgers have another pressing reason to get the rookie comfortable in the outfield.
If Ohtani and Dalton Rushing are able to return from the injured list prior to October, they can only occupy the roster as designated hitters or pinch hitters. That's a limiting factor in the postseason, when teams can only carry 26 active players in each round.
De Paula gives the Dodgers three left-handed hitting DHs — impractical at best, impossible at worst — unless he can play the outfield.
"He and Dino [Ebel, the Dodgers' outfielders coach] are committed to a routine, which I love,” Roberts said. “I think the other important thing is just so he can see how the quality and how intense the work is up here. And I think that you really don’t know until you know, and I’m excited for him to watch our guys, how they prepare each night.”

Edwin Diaz signed a three-year, $69 million contract in December. It made him baseball's highest-paid reliever by average annual salary. His first season for the Los Angeles Dodgers has not matched that price tag.
Diaz opened the year on a rocky note. He allowed one run through his first five outings. Two rough appearances followed.
Doctors then found loose bodies in his right elbow. He had arthroscopic surgery and missed roughly 100 days.
He returned in late July and posted mixed results. The Dodgers placed him back on the injured list Aug. 18. This time, doctors diagnosed inflammation on the right side of his neck.
Diaz has an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances this season. He has thrown 13 2/3 innings for the Los Angeles Dodgers. The right-hander has struck out 19 batters and walked 10.
That uneven form has created real uncertainty about his spot on the postseason roster.
Edwin Diaz's Roster Spot Now in Doubt
insider Ken Rosenthal addressed Diaz's situation on the show "Foul Territory." He said the Dodgers will pick their 26 best players, regardless of salary.
The club has called this year's pitching staff its deepest ever heading into October.
Rosenthal added that if evaluators view Diaz as not good enough, the Dodgers will leave him off. Rosenthal called it a "win-at-all-costs kind of industry."
Manager Dave Roberts has not guaranteed Diaz a spot either. "We have to go with our best pitchers," Roberts said. Diaz has not pitched well enough yet during his rehab assignment.
He allowed five runs while recording two outs in his Sept. 13 outing. He is set for another rehab appearance Sept. 16, with an expected return in late September.
The stakes are real. The Dodgers clinched a playoff berth Monday with a win over the Cincinnati Reds.
Latest Updates on Edwin Diaz, Shohei Ohtani
The Dodgers updated their injury report this week. Several key players remain sidelined heading into the stretch run.
Diaz remains on the 15-day injured list with neck inflammation. He is on a rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Shohei Ohtani is on the 15-day injured list with a left knee and right biceps injury, retroactive to Sept. 8. He could return as a hitter as soon as Sept. 23. He is not expected to pitch again until 2027. He began a swing progression Sept. 15, hitting off a tee.
Outfielder Andy Pages has a fractured left hand. He landed on the 10-day injured list Aug. 22. He has progressed to hitting baseballs off a machine, with an expected return in late September as well.

When he needed it most, starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto reminded everyone in the Los Angeles Dodgers clubhouse why he is the man for Game 1 of any playoff series.
A day after the Dodgers clinched their postseason berth and secured a shot at completing their three-peat, Yamamoto took the mound to help the team in their postseason seeding race with a road game against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday, September 16th.
Yamamoto went seven scoreless innings, allowing one hit and two walks while getting eight punchouts, and looked like he had much more in the tank.
Manager Dave Roberts could have easily kept Yamamoto in for at least another inning; the Japanese pitcher had only 91 pitches down, given his propensity to pitch a high volume.
He allowed only two hard hits, highlighting his dominance, and both walks came on his first two batters.
Yamamoto retired 21 of the final 22 batters he faced, threw 16 whiffs, and used a wide variety of pitches, with none exceeding 25% usage.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto had another great outing, his best one in a while:
7 IP
1 H
2 BB
7 Ks
He looked great and could have gone another inning on just 91 pitches.
Quick and efficient from the Dodgers' ace. pic.twitter.com/pro7lpwsiK
The outing was a nice change of pace for Yamamoto, who has been prone to the long ball and giving up hard contact.
Instead, he did a good job of keeping the Reds hitters off-balance, and it looked like what Dodger fans have come to expect from Yamamoto: efficiency, elite pitch mix, and weak contact.
Why Dave Roberts Trusts Yamamoto
More than anything, his ability to move on from mistakes, like his lack of command that led to two walks right off the bat, is really the special sauce for Yamamoto.
Roberts, after the game, spoke to this resilience and how it translates perfectly to October and high-leverage moments, when everyone gets tested in some shape or fashion.
"I think the thing that I've learned about Yoshinobu is he's able to reset on the fly," the skipper said.
"He's able to bear down and make pitches when he needs to, to get a double play, a strikeout, a pop-up.
"Those are separators. When you're not totally locked in or in sync, you can still take a deep breath, reset, and navigate an inning and keep going. And so that's something that I've really learned from him."
Why Yamamoto Needed This Outing Now
Given his 2025 postseason exploits, it is hard to argue that Yamamoto has much to prove in the playoffs, and he needs to make his case to pitch the first game in the postseason.
Pitching in Game 1, when the team is fully healthy, is the ultimate nod of respect for an ace, and earning that honor as a member of his special rotation makes it all the more noteworthy.
Yamamoto, given his track record, has seemingly been in pole position all season, but Blake Snell's form and Tarik Skubal's arrival have sparked a healthy debate about who takes the ball first.
Since returning from the IL after elbow surgery on August 11th, Snell has a 1.04 ERA through 34.2 innings. He has 46 strikeouts and 14 walks in that span.
Yamamoto has a 1.98 ERA in 68.1 innings since the All-Star break. His ratio is 72 strikeouts to 16 walks.
By comparison, Skubal has a 2.52 ERA in 50 innings with the Dodgers since joining from the trade deadline on August 3rd. He also has a 57 strikeouts-to-11 walks ratio.
Recently, Skubal had his own seven-inning scoreless outing, and he looked very settled in, while Snell has not put a foot wrong.
However, Yamamoto's latest outing showed the front office that he can deliver a vintage Yamamoto outing, which, come postseason time, is invaluable.
It means he can provide a long outing, sometimes a complete game, along with minimal runs allowed, and leave the hitters in a tizzy.

The Los Angeles Dodgers clinched a postseason spot for the 14th consecutive season and are closing in on a 13th National League West title during that span.
Also of importance for the Dodgers is finishing with a top two record in the NL as it would come with a first-round bye in the playoffs. That could be of particular value to a slew of injured Dodgers, including Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages, Dalton Rushing and Edgardo Henriquez.
Dodgers updates
Dalton Rushing
Rushing made a surprising return on Sept. 1 from a slight tear in the UCL of his right elbow, but only managed to appear in four games off the bench before going back on the 10-day injured list. That came after Rushing was scratched from the lineup due to right elbow trouble that stemmed from his attempt at a throwing progression.
The Dodgers have since ruled out Rushing possibly catching again this year, but they remain hopeful he will be an option as a left-handed bat off the bench.
“Dalton’s doing well,” manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA. “Building up his progression.”
Shohei Ohtani
Ohtani started his swinging progression on Tuesday by hitting off a tee. Roberts said he “felt good” doing so and is going to continue moving along.
“I don’t know what’s in store for tomorrow, but I know there’s going to be a consistent buildup. Don’t know when the time to return to play is, but today was positive and hopefully we can just keep building toward that,” Roberts said.
Roberts added he believes Ohtani will return at some point in the regular season, but cautioned, “Whether it happens or not is to be determined.”
Ohtani is eligible to be activated off the 15-day injured list Sept. 23.
Andy Pages
Pages has been swinging a bat for several days and took a step forward on Tuesday by hitting off pitching machine. Next for Pages is to log at-bats against the Trajekt machine.
Edgardo Henriquez
Henriquez, the latest Dodgers injury, returned to Los Angeles in order to undergo testing on his back/side area. He was officially put on the 15-day injured list due to low back discomfort, but Roberts noted there might be some trouble with the oblique as well.
Henriquez is not eligible to return during the regular season but the Dodgers hope he will be available for the playoffs.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Josue De Paula is in his element in the batter’s box. He carries himself like a guy who knows his importance to the Los Angeles Dodgers depends on how well he can command himself within those 24 square feet of chalk lines. De Paula asserts himself with a confident shake of the head after each pitch outside the strike zone.
Advertisement
Some head shakes are more exaggerated than others. Each demonstrates the same message: De Paula is not going to give in.
“I just want to feel saucy when I’m up there, you know what I’m saying?” De Paula told The Athletic this week. “I feel like I’m in control, not you. … I want my pitch. Come in the zone. Let’s go.”
This is who De Paula wants to be. He describes hitting as “aggressive patience,” an approach that puts him on the attack.
“It’s almost like a war for me in my head,” De Paula said. “I look confident. I look saucy. I feel saucy when I’m in the box, so it’s like, ‘Hey bro, let’s keep it rocking.’”
It took four games for De Paula to inspire fascination within the Dodgers dynasty, where his every at-bat feels like a must-watch example of how to command a zone. Of the first 37 big-league pitches De Paula saw outside of the strike zone, he swung at just five. He made it 17 plate appearances without striking out before going down swinging in the seventh inning and looking in the ninth in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Reds on Tuesday. De Paula does not seem fazed that he is just 2 for 14 (.143) since being called up, including five hitless at-bats in his first game in the leadoff spot.
That’s because he believes in his process. A day earlier, De Paula battled back from down in the count against Reds lefty Nick Lodolo, a former All-Star. The left-handed batter took a 2-2 fastball just below the knees, crouched and shook his head. A pitch later, De Paula walked for the fifth time in his short career.
The clip of the head shake drew a chuckle from the proprietor of the “Soto Shuffle” himself, Juan Soto, who, like De Paula, once honed his craft at the El Niche Baseball Academy in the Dominican city of Santo Domingo.
Josue De Paula live reaction to you trying to get him to chase. https://t.co/CrmRSnDVgO pic.twitter.com/dbXGz8WYL0
— Chad Moriyama (@ChadMoriyama) September 14, 2026
“El loco mío,” Soto shared to his Instagram story in Spanish, stamping his approval with a laughing emoji. My guy.
Advertisement
“I swear I wasn’t trying to do like the whole thing,” De Paula said with a laugh. “I just got into my legs, and I was shaking my head … but I’m not mad. That’s not a bad player to look like.”
De Paula, 21, feels like an injection of youthful exuberance for baseball’s oldest lineup. The Brooklyn-born son of a Dominican father (and relative of NBA veterans Stephon Marbury and Sebastian Telfair) speaks with a thick New York accent and oozes the confidence of a player who carries that swagger into the box.
De Paula is the crown jewel of a Dodgers farm system that is expected to prolong this run of excellence. Last week, he became the first position player ever to be called up directly from Double A by this Andrew Friedman-led front office group.
De Paula is here because he can hit, has always hit, and the Dodgers need him to hit. De Paula is here to serve as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, at least until Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list. No one with the Dodgers, however, is ruling out the possibility that De Paula could help them in October as they seek a third consecutive World Series title.
“I hope he makes our decision hard,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Through De Paula’s torrid run through the Dodgers’ farm system, officials raved about his keen ability to pick up the baseball, make proper swing decisions and recognize spin.
“He doesn’t give away any pitches, which I love, let alone give away any at-bats,” Roberts said.
Pair that with a preternatural ability to make contact, and De Paula entered this season as one of the highly-regarded young hitters in the league. The Dodgers implemented a change to De Paula’s swing this year, lowering his hands and opening up his resulting bat path to keep the barrel in the zone longer. That has allowed him to access more power by pulling more fly balls and has made him a lethal producer at Double A.
Advertisement
De Paula slugged 27 home runs this season in Double A, more than double what he had in any of his first four professional seasons. His first hit Sunday in Miami was a mammoth upper-deck shot to right field on the kind of awe-inspiring swing that has come much more easily for De Paula than in years past.
“When all those things are kind of clicking, it’s tough for any pitcher to compete with,” hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc said. “So it’s been very impressive so far.”
De Paula became a Dodger partially as a byproduct of the COVID-19 pandemic, which shut down the New York baseball season and prompted De Paula’s father, Josue Sr., to send him to the Dominican Republic to work at El Niche under Cristian “Niche” Batista.
“It was like stepping into a whole other world,” De Paula said.
It was there, during an offseason workout, that De Paula met Soto, who broke into the big leagues at 19 years old with the kind of swaggering command of the batter’s box that De Paula hopes to replicate. Rather than enter the amateur draft, De Paula signed directly with the Dodgers as an international amateur for a bonus of just under $400,000. De Paula estimated that, in one of his two tryouts with the organization and with several of the club’s brass in attendance, he collected nine hits in 10 at-bats.
“I killed,” De Paula said, reliving the memory as if it just happened.
He has hit ever since, ascending to the top of prospect lists. His list of star-studded admirers grew, too. After accompanying Soto in being represented by super agent Scott Boras, De Paula was asked by Boras to name some of his favorite players. De Paula selected Elly De La Cruz, who at that time was set for his first season as a breakout star for the Cincinnati Reds but was already dominating the minor leagues. Boras invited De Paula to his Newport Beach offices in Southern California after that and surprised him by bringing De La Cruz.
Advertisement
The two have remained close, working out together in the Miami area in the winters. Friday, just before he made his major-league debut against the Marlins in Miami, De Paula called De La Cruz on FaceTime. When they met up again this week in Cincinnati, they posed for a picture.
“I’m really happy for what he’s doing,” De La Cruz said.
De Paula sees a kinship between De La Cruz and Soto.
“We’re all killers,” De Paula said with a knowing smirk.
When De Paula spent his first spring training in big-league camp with the Dodgers in 2025, he quickly heard from Mookie Betts. The former Gold Glove right fielder wanted to make De Paula and fellow newcomers Zyhir Hope and Justin Dean feel welcome, so over dinner at a Phoenix-area soul food restaurant, he talked shop. When De Paula went out for early defensive work in the outfield this week, he had Roberts and Betts at different points offer some advice.
Now in a clubhouse filled with stars, De Paula said he feels at home. Whether he stays there heading into October will depend on how the rest of the regular season goes. The first few games have left a strong first impression.
“It’s a slow heartbeat,” Van Scoyoc said. “He’s not overwhelmed at all. It seemed like he picked up where he left off in Double A. … I wouldn’t say it’s surprising, but it’s just nice to see.”
Ohtani is expected to return from his nagging biceps and knee injuries by year’s end. De Paula has a lack of defensive utility at this point. While he did play in left field on Sunday, the Dodgers still want to work on getting De Paula to “value” the defensive side of the ball first, Roberts said. That means his path to the Dodgers’ postseason roster will likely be as a left-handed bat off the bench, essentially the role the club envisioned for Dalton Rushing before his most recent IL stint.
Advertisement
That decision is still up in the air, Roberts said. There will be “growing pains,” as Roberts said after Tuesday’s performance. The manager said he “didn’t love” the quality of De Paula’s at-bats. But October is a scenario De Paula feels he will be ready for.
“Especially in big moments, I feel like my mind just goes to a whole ‘nother level,” De Paula said. “Especially competing. The bigger the moment is … it’s like the more my mind hyper-focuses. So when I’m hyper-focused like that a lot, it’s dangerous.”

How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — A simple change opened a dramatic offensive turnaround for Dodgers left fielder Teoscar Hernández.
Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday, in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win against the Reds, was his second home run in as many nights, as the team trimmed its magic number to clinch the division to one behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s seven innings of one-hit ball. And, significantly, this one was against a right-handed pitcher.
“It’s been very helpful,” manager Dave Roberts said after the game. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. And the last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him.”
Through the end of August, Hernández had just a .668 OPS against right-handed pitchers this season. So, when Roberts was asked in Detroit whether the Dodgers would consider setting up a left-field platoon with the team’s September call-ups, he said yes.
Hernández homered off Tigers left-hander Framber Valdez on the last day of the series. And before the Dodgers opened a three-game set against the Cardinals at Dodger Stadium, Hernández met with the hitting coaches.
Against Valdez, Hernández was in a closed stance, to delay his front hip from opening, according to Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates. But the team’s hitting group thought a return to a familiar setup could be a long-term solution.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
In the past, Hernández had used a “twister tap” as his stride. He started in a more open stance, tapped his toe in line with the pitcher, and then set his foot down. But lower-body injuries the last couple of years — a left groin strain last season and a left hamstring strain earlier this season — forced him away from it.
His improved health and hip flexibility opened the avenue for him to return to that timing mechanism.
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
The advantage of the twister tap, as Hernández explained it, is how repeatable it is. A more traditional stride can be sped up or slowed down.
“Just being able to control my body and being in a good position,” Hernández said earlier this month. “I can see the pitch a little sooner and identify what kind of pitch it is and if it’s going to be a strike or a ball.”
With that change, he’s rewarded the Dodgers for deciding against platooning left field. Hernández entered Tuesday with a .777 OPS against right-handed pitchers — a sample size of just 28 plate appearances but still a significant jump.
“The biggest thing is his plate coverage away,” Bates said. “Because now he can spoil pitches, and he’s staying in at-bats longer.”
Hernández’s dramatic offensive turnaround, along with fellow corner outfielder Kyle Tucker’s improvement, have helped steady a Dodgers offense that’s missing Shohei Ohtani (on the IL with right biceps and left knee injuries) and includes a hobbled Freddie Freeman (right knee soreness).
Rookie Josue De Paula, mostly filling in for Ohtani at designated hitter, has already shown he can take mature at-bats and provide some pop. But he’s still finding his footing in a new league.
It lengthens the Dodgers lineup for Hernández, after a slow start to his year, to return to being a veteran power threat — just in time to, ideally, carry the momentum into the postseason.
On Monday, he launched his two-run shot off left-hander Nick Lodolo. On Tuesday, he replicated the feat off right-hander Rhett Lowder.
On the second pitch of the at-bat, Hernández recognized a hung slider, and he roped it over the left-field fence at 109.3 mph, according to Statcast. The blast put the Dodgers up 3-0 in the third inning, with Dodgers starter Yamamoto settling into a groove on the other side.
Yamamoto had walked the first two batters he faced, but he reined in his control to pitch seven scoreless innings and allow just one more baserunner — a double by Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz.
The Dodgers also scored on Hunter Feduccia’s second-inning single and Alex Freeland’s seventh-inning homer. And the Dodgers bullpen completed the shutout.
Freeman staying in the lineup
Freeman was all smiles after his three-hit game Tuesday — after going hitless for his last four games.
“I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there,” he said. “So I’m very excited.”
Roberts explained: “He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’”
Sure enough, the mechanical adjustments he made in the batting cage — focusing on getting his foot down early and making contact out in front — got him there.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results,” Freeman said. “We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable.”
Though Roberts has been trying to find opportunities to rest Freeman, he saw promising signs Tuesday beyond the results.
“Just my eyes, just watching him move, I feel good about him going tomorrow,” Roberts said.
De Paula, Freeland and third baseman Max Muncy will be out of the lineup Wednesday, Roberts said.

Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani took swings off a tee Tuesday as he works toward returning from the injured list before the playoffs.
“Shohei hit off the tee and felt good today,” manager Dave Roberts said before Los Angeles defeated the host Cincinnati Reds 4-0. “I don’t know what’s in store for him tomorrow, but I know that there’s going to be a consistent build-up. Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return and play in some regular-season games before shifting to the playoffs.
“Whether it happens or not is to be determined, but I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games,” Roberts said. “I don’t know how many.”
Ohtani, 32, was placed on the injured list to rest his left knee and right biceps. Soreness in those areas, along with a neck issue, caused him to miss four straight games earlier this month, but the Dodgers initially hoped to avoid an IL stint.
Because Ohtani is a two-way player, he must be on the IL for a minimum of 15 days. Sept. 23 is the soonest he can be activated. The Dodgers will have five games to go in the regular season at that point — two against the San Diego Padres at home and a three-game road series at the San Francisco Giants.
Overall this year, the six-time All-Star is hitting .277 with a .380 on-base percentage, a .522 slugging percentage, 30 homers and 80 RBIs in 130 games.

CINCINNATI — For the first time in what’s felt like a while, the Dodgers’ usually foreboding daily injury updates came with some needed signs of optimism on Tuesday.
Before the game, manager Dave Roberts said two-way star Shohei Ohtani “felt good” after resuming hitting activities on Monday, when he took swings off a tee back in Los Angeles. And while Roberts didn’t guarantee Ohtani would return from the injured list before the end of the regular season, that at least remains the team’s expectation for now.
“Today was positive,” Roberts said, “and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Then, in an even bigger development, first baseman Freddie Freeman not only returned to the lineup in Tuesday night’s win over the Cincinnati Reds, but put together a three-hit performance that “played myself in” to Wednesday’s lineup, he proudly noted with a grin.
Initially, Roberts was planning to rest Freeman on Wednesday amid his ongoing battle with a right knee injury. That would have marked the 37-year-old’s fourth missed game out of the last seven for the team.
Early in the night, however, Freeman struck a deal with his manager.
“He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’” Roberts recounted.
Right on cue, Freeman lined singles in the first, fifth and seventh innings — snapping out of his troubling 3-for-30 slump previously.
“It looked good,” Roberts said. “It looked more like Freddie.”
Not only did the veteran slugger feel no pain in his knee — where he has been battling a patellar tendinitis problem — but he also revealed a fruitful adjustment he had made before the game with his swing.
Amid his recent knee problems, Freeman felt he had started letting the ball travel too far in his stance before beginning his swing, causing him to “slide” in the box, especially with a compromised front leg.
Thus, he made a temporary change he hopes will spark him ahead of the playoffs, focusing on getting his front leg down sooner and catching the ball further out at the front of his swing.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep,” he said. “So today was [get the] foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit, and it kind of worked. I wasn’t squaring the ball up in the game, but I’ll take those three hits and keep that work going tomorrow, and hopefully we’ll get hot.”
It’s not a permanent solution, Freeman noted. But at this point in the year, “I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable,” he said. “I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
Indeed, between that and Ohtani’s progress — which has the Dodgers remaining cautiously optimistic about his chances to make an impact in the playoffs — it was enough for the team to finally feel some optimism about the way they are trending toward October, getting a couple of positive updates on two of their superstar hitters.

Teoscar Hernández volvió a demostrar que atraviesa un momento ofensivo importante y encabezó la ofensiva de los Dodgers en la victoria 4-0 sobre los Reds este martes en el Great American Ball Park.
El dominicano conectó un cuadrangular de dos carreras en la tercera entrada, su segundo vuelacercas en igual cantidad de partidos, para ampliar una ventaja que Los Ángeles ya no perdería.
Hernández terminó de 3-1 y produjo dos carreras, mientras los Dodgers se acercaron a solo dos victorias de asegurar el título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional.
El jonrón tuvo además un significado particular para Hernández, quien había tenido dificultades frente a los lanzadores derechos durante buena parte de la temporada. Hasta finales de agosto, registraba apenas .668 de OPS contra derechos, situación que incluso llevó al manager Dave Roberts a considerar un posible pelotón en el jardín izquierdo con jugadores recién ascendidos.
Después de conectar un jonrón ante el zurdo Framber Valdez en Detroit, Hernández trabajó con los coaches de bateo antes de la serie contra los Cardinals, y desde entonces su producción ha comenzado a cambiar.
Yamamoto intransitable
La actuación del dominicano sirvió como complemento perfecto para otra extraordinaria presentación de Yoshinobu Yamamoto. El japonés tuvo un comienzo poco habitual, al fallar ocho de sus primeros nueve lanzamientos y conceder boletos consecutivos a los dos primeros bateadores de Cincinnati. Fue apenas la cuarta ocasión esta temporada en que otorgó múltiples boletos en una entrada y la primera vez en su carrera de Grandes Ligas que abrió una salida con dos bases por bolas consecutivas.
Pero aquel descontrol inicial quedó rápidamente en el pasado. Después de poner a dos corredores en las bases en el primer episodio, Yamamoto solo permitió que otro bateador de Cincinnati llegara a salvo durante el resto de su actuación. Retiró a 21 de los últimos 22 bateadores que enfrentó y completó siete entradas en blanco, con apenas un hit permitido, un doble de Elly De La Cruz en el tercer inning, además de siete ponches.
La ofensiva angelina había tomado ventaja desde el segundo episodio, cuando Hunter Feduccia produjo una carrera con un sencillo. En el tercero llegó el batazo de Hernández para colocar el marcador 3-0 y, posteriormente, Alex Freeland agregó otro cuadrangular solitario para completar las cuatro carreras de Los Ángeles. El ataque de los Dodgers no fue especialmente abundante, pero produjo lo suficiente para respaldar a Yamamoto y convertir su actuación en una nueva joya monticular.
Para Yamamoto, fue además su tercera apertura consecutiva completando siete entradas y la quinta salida seguida en la que alcanzó al menos el séptimo episodio. Desde la pausa del Juego de Estrellas, el derecho japonés ha mantenido un ritmo dominante, con efectividad de 1.98 en 68? entradas, 72 ponches y solo 16 boletos en 10 aperturas, una producción que lo coloca como una de las principales piezas de la rotación de Los Ángeles de cara a octubre.
La victoria dejó a los Dodgers con el número mágico en dos para conquistar su decimotercer título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional en las últimas 14 temporadas.
- Después de haber asegurado ya su boleto a la postemporada, Los Ángeles continúa ahora en busca de la corona divisional y de una posición privilegiada para octubre.
Blake Snell será el encargado de subir al montículo en el próximo encuentro de la serie, mientras los Dodgers siguen construyendo una rotación que, con Yamamoto al frente, vuelve a tomar protagonismo en su búsqueda de un tercer campeonato consecutivo.

CINCINNATI — The Dodgers can only hope it looks this good in October.
One night after Tarik Skubal went seven innings in his first scoreless outing as a Dodger, Yoshinobu Yamamoto matched him, allowing only one hit in his seven scoreless innings as the Dodgers shut out the Cincinnati Reds, 4-0, on Tuesday night.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going tomorrow – you feel good about preventing runs,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
The win moved the Dodgers (92-59) within one day of clinching their 13th NL West division title in the past 14 seasons. Their magic number is one after the second-place San Diego Padres (82-69) lost to the Colorado Rockies later Tuesday night.
The Dodgers’ lead over the Atlanta Braves (89-63) for the No. 2 seed in the National League remains 3½ games. Their magic number to clinch a first-round bye is eight.
All of that makes the final two weeks of the regular season a chance for the Dodgers to get things right for October and their three-peat pursuit. The starting rotation appears to be there already.
Skubal has a 1.73 ERA over his past four starts. With Tuesday’s outing, Yamamoto’s ERA is 1.79 over his past seven starts. Blake Snell starts on Wednesday – and he has given up a total of only four runs in six starts since returning from elbow surgery. Only fourth starter Tyler Glasnow (eight runs in 10 innings over his past two starts) seems to have some work to do before being October-ready.
“Yeah, pretty good,” first baseman Freddie Freeman said after his first three-hit game since Aug. 17. “You have Blake Snell going tomorrow. Tyler on the back end of that too. Roki’s on his way back.
“It’s a special pitching staff. It really is. So as an offense, we just need to score a few runs for them, just like we did last year.”
Yamamoto started Tuesday by giving the Reds hope – he walked the first two batters he faced – then he took it away, retiring 21 of the next 22 batters he faced.
“They took a little moment for me,” Yamamoto said through his interpreter of the mound visit from catcher Hunter Feduccia and pitching coach Mark Prior that followed the walks. “They came up to me and, ‘Hey, how you doing?’ and just checked in on me. And then I was able to get back to my normal rhythm.”
Elly De La Cruz had the only hit off Yamamoto, a double into the left-field corner with two outs in the third inning.
But even that was a victory – Yamamoto kept him in the ballpark after De La Cruz had hit a home run in each of the previous four games between the Dodgers and Reds. He then retired the next 13 batters in order, getting six of his seven strikeouts.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine. Not giving these guys too much credit. And yeah, at first, it didn’t look promising as far as pitch count, the two walks. But then he kind of dialed things in, like he’s been known to do.”
The Dodgers gave him a lead in the second inning when Max Muncy was hit by a pitch and Tommy Edman and Hunter Feduccia followed with singles. They added to it in the third inning with a two-run home run from Teoscar Hernandez, who remains hot – 24 for 63 (.381) in his past 18 games.
“It’s been very helpful,” Roberts said of Hernandez’s late-season renaissance. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. The last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him. The defense ticked up. The at-bat quality, the taking walks, all of it. I can’t say enough about what he’s done the last 10 days.”

Edwin Díaz deberá ganarse la confianza de Dave Roberts para lanzar con los Dodgers en la postemporada
El dirigente de Los Ángeles puso en duda la participación del relevista tras un primer año complicado con los bicampeones.
PUBLICIDAD
El cerrador puertorriqueño Edwin “Sugar” Díaz deberá ganarse su espacio en el roster de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles para poder treparse al montículo durante la postemporada, informó el mánager Dave Roberts en un aparte con la prensa estadounidense.
Díaz ha tenido un primer año complicado tras firmar un contrato de tres campañas y $69 millones con los Dodgers en la temporada muerta. Posee marca de 2-2, siete salvamentos, una errática efectividad de 11.85 en 13.2 entradas lanzadas durante 16 apariciones y ha desperdiciado cuatro de sus 11 oportunidades de salvamento.
También ha permitido 18 carreras, tres de ellas en el noveno inning de su última presentación frente a los Rockies de Colorado el pasado 17 de agosto. Al día siguiente entró a la lista de lesionados por una inflamación en el cuello.
Actualmente se encuentra en una asignación de rehabilitación con los Comets de Oklahoma City, filial de los Dodgers en Triple A. Sin embargo, lo que apuntaba a ser una corta estadía en las Menores para recuperar su nivel ha generado aún más interrogantes sobre el naguabeño, quien hace unos años era considerado uno de los mejores relevistas de las Mayores.
Díaz cargó el domingo con la más reciente derrota de Oklahoma City al permitir cinco carreras y conceder tres bases por bolas ante los Space Cowboys, filial de los Astros de Houston. El derecho pudo retirar a un solo bateador.
Por actuaciones como esas, Roberts entiende que el boricua aún no ha recuperado su nivel y evitó comprometerse cuando la prensa le preguntó si estará entre los lanzadores seleccionados para la postemporada.
Dave Roberts on Edwin Diaz's rehab assignment, via @SonjaMChen:
"He needs to pitch better. It hasn't been good."
Diaz rehab assignment so far:
3.1 IP, 6 ER, 4 K, 3 H, 7 BB pic.twitter.com/304XoBbDsU
“Necesita lanzar mejor. No lo ha hecho bien. Lanzará el miércoles y supongo que lo evaluaremos entonces”, dijo el dirigente de los Dodgers.
“Lo tengo en muy alta estima, pero en esta situación tiene que haber algo que nos dé motivos para estar seguros y él lo sabe. Quiere lanzar bien. Así que, por mi parte, el miércoles lo observaremos con atención”, abundó.
Díaz subirá a la loma el miércoles contra los Chihuahuas de El Paso, filial de los Padres de San Diego en las Menores. La llegada del tres veces seleccionado al Juego de Estrellas a Los Ángeles generó grandes expectativas, ya que era visto como el relevista que le daría a Roberts la seguridad que no tuvo su bullpen en campañas anteriores.
En cambio, el primer año del naguabeño vistiendo el uniforme de Los Ángeles ha estado marcado por lesiones, incluida una en el codo derecho que requirió una intervención quirúrgica y que lo mantuvo fuera por más de tres meses. Aun así, el piloto de los bicampeones continúa apostando en Díaz.
“Tenemos que ir con nuestros mejores lanzadores en términos de rendimiento, talento y todo eso”, indicó Roberts.
“Mi apuesta es que (Díaz) estará (incluido en el roster), pero, nuevamente, tiene que haber algún tipo de evidencia o algo que nos permita confiar en él. Mi apuesta es que sí, pero todavía tenemos que ver algo”, continuó.
Los Dodgers clasificaron el lunes a la postemporada con una victoria sobre los Reds de Cincinnati. Será su decimocuarta aparición consecutiva en los playoffs, empatando así el récord de las Grandes Ligas que los Braves de Atlanta establecieron entre 1991 y 2005. Además, lideran la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional con marca de 91-59.

CINCINNATI –– Every day, Tarik Skubal learns something new about playing for the Dodgers.
Monday's lesson: Clinching a playoff spot warrants only subtle celebrations.
"It's different than anything I've experienced, for sure," Skubal chuckled on Monday night, after the Dodgers recognized their 14th consecutive postseason berth with only a subdued postgame champagne toast and brief speech from manager Dave Roberts.
"But," the club's new star pitcher added, "I think it just speaks to the people in this room and what they expect out of this team. That was cool. A little toast and move on. Forget it happened. We've got more to accomplish this season."
Consider it the latest step in Skubal's acclimation process with the Dodgers –– another little moment that made him feel more at home with his new team.
He's now six weeks on from his emotional trade from the Detroit Tigers at the deadline.
And he's starting to find a comfort level that, after an uneven start to his Dodgers tenure, is helping him look more like the star pitcher he is accustomed to being.
"Constantly learning each other and developing relationships –– a lot of that stuff you don't realize, no one writes about that kind of relationship –– but I think it matters, it matters a lot. I probably underestimated that a little bit," said Skubal, who had spent the entirety of his career in Detroit before his marquee move to the Dodgers.
"But just communicating, having an open dialogue with everyone, all these guys, on what I like to do, what I'm comfortable with and honestly what I'm uncomfortable with … I think we're developing a real good relationship," he added.
And as a result, as manager Dave Roberts noted, "I think the last couple [outings he has made] have been his best."
That was certainly true on Monday, when Skubal spun a gem with the Dodgers' postseason berth in the balance.
He delivered his first scoreless start with the team by blanking the Reds over seven innings at Great American Ball Park. He gave up just three hits and one walk while striking out nine batters in a 90-pitch domination.
"To take the mound on the night that we had a chance to clinch, and we did it," Roberts said, "I think that's something he should be proud of."
More important to Skubal was the way it reflected his growing familiarity with the Dodgers' catchers and pitching department.
He noted he only shook Will Smith off one time all night. He praised the rhythm he has developed with pitching coaches in pre-game prep meetings. And he credited it all with helping him eliminate some perfectionist tendencies that hampered his first month with the team (when he gave up nine runs in 24 innings while lacking the ruthless efficiency that made him a reigning back-to-back Cy Young Award winner).
"I think a lot of the struggles have been 'me vs. me,' thinking too much out there and not competing the way I know how to compete," Skubal said. "Sometimes I try to be too perfect with things instead of just attacking guys over the middle of the plate and letting my stuff play, especially early in games, behind in the count, just not trying to be too fine."
To put it more simply, Skubal added, it was a process of "trying to find the rhythm of who I know I am."
And to people around the team, it's no coincidence that has happened as he's carved out a place in his new clubhouse, as well.
"He's just chill," pitching coach Mark Prior said. "You can joke around with him. You can talk to him."
Few players have grown closer with Skubal than Blake Snell to this point. They've sat side-by-side in the dugout during games, locked in constant conversation. They were pulling practical jokes on one another Tuesday, knocking over each other's chairs in the clubhouse. They've even begun making Step Brothers-inspired jokes about being new best friends on social media.
"I think we're best friends," Snell deadpanned. "Some days, he agrees."
Snell told the California Post that their relationship blossomed naturally, with Snell immediately being struck by how Skubal was "very confident and very secure with who he is" even amid new surroundings.
Two other observations:
"I didn't think he was that funny," Snell joked, describing a side of Skubal that came out Monday night when he razzed backup catcher Hunter Feduccia about a snazzy short-sleeve dress shirt and matching pair of brown slacks ("Outfit of the day!" Skubal declared).
"And," Snell added, "I like how competitive he is. Because it just makes both of us so much better."
That latter dynamic could fuel the Dodgers' entire rotation moving forward, especially entering a postseason in which the group will likely have to carry the team.
"Every time one of our boys go, we want them to dominate, and then the next man up wants to do even better," Snell said. "I think that's very important, to know that we're supporting each other and we're pushing each other to be great, and that we're not focused on just our own achievements. We're focused on our group of starting pitchers all succeeding."
Prior echoed those sentiments, noting that with Skubal specifically: "He wants to have fun. And he wants to win."
Lately, Skubal has been, now on a four-start stretch with only five runs allowed in his last 26 innings.
For the Dodgers, it's a sign of his growth process since being acquired by the club; one that could prove crucial in their three-peat ambitions.
"It's hard to get in that rhythm [and develop] that trust," Roberts said. "But for me, I see just more of the trust in whatever is called, and then you can just go out there [be himself]."

CINCINNATI -- Shohei Ohtani resumed swinging on Tuesday for the first time since landing on the 15-day injured list last week, manager Dave Roberts said before the Dodgers' game against the Reds at Great American Ball Park.
Ohtani is not on the road with the Dodgers, but he hit off a tee in L.A. and came away feeling good afterward, Roberts said. It was Ohtani's first time swinging since his lingering right biceps and left knee injuries led him to be shut down starting last Wednesday.
"I don't know what's in store for tomorrow, but I know that there's going to be a consistent buildup," Roberts said. "Don't know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that."
Ohtani's 15-day IL placement is backdated to Sept. 8, meaning that the earliest he can be activated is Sept. 23, with five regular-season games remaining for the Dodgers. Roberts believes that Ohtani will be back in action before the end of the regular season.
"Whether it happens or not is to be determined, but I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games," Roberts said. "Don't know how many of them."
In his last 24 games, a span that coincided with an attempt to ramp up as a pitcher, Ohtani hit .198 (19-for-96) with a .690 OPS and 34 strikeouts. Toward the end of that stretch, he began to look physically compromised at the plate, leading the Dodgers to leave him out of the lineup for four straight games. He returned to the lineup on Sept. 7 but did not come away from that game feeling good.
At that point, the Dodgers opted to place Ohtani on the IL with the aim of getting him right for the postseason. He will return only as a hitter, with his two-way duties shelved until 2027.
The Dodgers have fared well without their best hitter, entering Tuesday having won nine of the 11 games they played since Ohtani was first held out of the lineup on Sept. 3. They clinched their record-tying 14th consecutive postseason berth on Monday and are close to winning their 13th NL West title in that span, all while remaining in position to secure a first-round bye.
The understanding is that Ohtani will probably not feel 100 percent in the postseason, but he'll use the weeks ahead to feel as good as he can, both physically and with his swing. While the Dodgers have gotten by without him, they know they'll need whatever they can get from him as they bid for a three-peat.

Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Roki Sasaki’s regular-season status is unclear, according to Dave Roberts.
The Dodgers are trying to determine whether Sasaki will pitch again before the regular season wraps up or if his next outing will come in the postseason as a reliever.
Sasaki has been battling a blister, and he has thrown some bullpen sessions, but he is not ready to return yet, Roberts said.
Per the skipper, he will throw in a simulated game on Wednesday, September 16th, before the team decides whether he can pitch this season.
Originally, the Dodgers were hopeful Sasaki would pitch as early as Thursday, according to The Athletic’s Katie Woo, but that is no longer the case under Dave Roberts’ new timeline.
Only a handful of games remain in the regular season, and if he doesn’t pitch this week, he has only one other week left to pitch.
It seems there may not be a soft landing for the young Japanese pitcher, and he will be asked to jump headfirst into a role he is familiar with.
Why Sasaki’s setback may not be a big deal
This season, Roki Sasaki has pitched 119.1 innings in 23 games, so he will not be battling much rust.
Additionally, he hasn’t been totally shut down for long; he got treatment for the blister and has diligently ramped up his recovery.
Sasaki will not enter the postseason cold, and he has pitched out of the bullpen before, notably in the 2025 postseason when he was the closer.
While he may be asked to be the setup man rather than the closer, he should still have plenty of experience to draw on before the playoffs begin.

Kyle Tucker's home run Monday in Cincinnati was his third in his last five games. In that span he's raised his slugging percentage from a season-low .350 on Sept. 8 to .376 entering Tuesday's rematch against the Reds.
September is halfway through, and it's shaping into Tucker's best month of the season. If it seems like he's stopped pressing at the plate, perhaps Tucker let up on himself after getting some needed reassurance in a one-on-one meeting with Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
“I told him, I’m gonna ride or die with him,” Roberts said (via Jack Harris of the California Post). “That was my young term phrase.”
It's been a rough ride for Tucker in his first season in Los Angeles. The Dodgers signed the four-time All-Star to a four-year, $240 million contract over the winter. Despite being baseball's highest-paid player this season, Tucker hit only one home run in his first 17 games of the season.
Things didn't get much better from there. Among 138 qualified hitters through the end of August, Tucker's .683 OPS ranked 116th.
"I was prepared, the organization was prepared, to give him as much leash as we possibly could to work through some things, and I do think that now we’re starting to see the fruits,” Roberts said. “So I see no other reason why we would pivot from running him out there every day.”
Fans might beg to differ.
At Triple-A Oklahoma City, outfielder James Tibbs III has 29 home runs and 101 RBIs to go with a .417 on-base percentage. Prospect Josue De Paula, who's played right field in the minors, was promoted to take Shohei Ohtani's place on the active roster.
Since his debut, the 21-year-old has reached base in half of his first 14 plate appearances. Sunday, he hit his first career home run. Perhaps Roberts needed to reassure Tucker that De Paula wasn't coming for his job to unlock his production, a curious case of reverse psychology.
It will be hard for the Dodgers to take De Paula out of the lineup if he maintains his current level of production. Roberts said prior to Ohtani's IL stint that the team wasn't considering using him in the outfield.
Tucker, for his part, can reduce the Dodgers' temptation to use Ohtani or De Paula in right field if he continues to hit like a $60 million All-Star.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are in familiar territory with the playoffs less than two weeks away. They are once again looking for answers in their bullpen. The Dodgers have placed Edgardo Henriquez on the IL with lower back discomfort, and he has been ruled out for the remainder of the regular season.
Henriquez has been placed on the 15-day IL, but there remains a path for him returning during the playoffs if all goes well. While the Dodgers made Edwin Diaz a priority this past offseason, it has been Henriquez who has kept the bullpen together.
Through 61 appearances, Henriquez had a 2.85 ERA while striking out over 29% of the hitters he's faced. If he's unable to return to LA's bullpen during the playoffs, the unit is suddenly facing a problem.
Edgardo Henriquez injury leaves Dodgers facing reality they desperately wanted to avoid
While the Dodgers have a healthy amount of left-handed options in the bullpen — considering Tanner Scott once again becoming an effective option at the end of games — as well as Alex Vesia and Jack Dreyer, they don't really have an established option among righties.
Brock Stewart hasn't looked bad this season, but injuries have limited him to just 22 innings pitched this season. Evan Phillips is back in the bullpen, and while he has 3.68 ERA through 27 appearances, his FIP of 4.65 makes him a regression candidate ahead of the playoffs.
It also doesn't help matters that the Dodgers aren't viewing the return of Diaz as a potential solution. He is currently on a minor-league rehab assignment, but the results simply haven't been there. It's forced Dave Roberts to offer a blunt assessment on Diaz earlier this week, suggesting there's a chance he's left off the playoff roster if he can't overcome his current struggles.
That is why Henriquez's injury is such a blow. He was a clear answer for what the Dodgers lacked in the bullpen, and coupling that with Diaz's struggles, Roberts and Co. are back at the drawing board. Perhaps Kris Bubic could be an answer. Bubic is with the Dodgers after a successful rehab assignment earlier this month and is expected to be reinstated from the IL in the coming days.
If there is a silver lining for the Dodgers, outside of Shohei Ohtani, their starting rotation is healthy and that could ultimately prove to be the difference-maker during the playoffs.

The Los Angeles Dodgers shortstop Mookie Betts is producing a new movie. On Monday, he announced the project away from the field. He's producing a movie titled "Cannon Street All-Stars."
Los Angeles clinched a playoff berth the same day, beating the Cincinnati Reds 4-1. The win pushed them to 91-59 with 12 games left. It marks the Dodgers' 14th straight postseason appearance.
However, Betts did little to contribute to that win. He went 0-for-4. No hits, home runs or RBIs.
He is having a down year by his standards.
Betts is batting .248 with 20 home runs, 62 RBIs and 108 hits this season. His career average sits at .288. Betts won AL MVP in 2018 and has made eight All-Star teams.
Off the diamond, however, he is excelling in his projects.
More on Mookie Betts' Latest Project
Betts is producing the film alongside Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry, Deadline reported in an exclusive Monday.
Director Reggie Rock Bythewood and his wife, Gina Prince-Bythewood, are developing the project through their company, Undisputed Cinema. Bythewood will write and direct.
The film tells the true story of the Cannon Street YMCA All-Stars. The all-Black Little League team from Charleston, South Carolina, tried to enter the 1955 state tournament.
Little League baseball in the South remained segregated at the time, eight years after Jackie Robinson broke MLB's color line. The team's push sparked forfeits and national attention. The Jackie Robinson Foundation backs the project.
Bythewood called the film overdue recognition. Surviving players were honored at last year's Little League World Series. "Now it is time to honor them on film," Bythewood said.
Betts produces through his company, OMG Entertainment, alongside Cam Lewis and Omar Bradford. Curry produces through Unanimous Media with Sharla Sumpter Bridgett. Debra Martin Chase and E. Monique Floyd also produce.
Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman Latest Updates
Despite clinching the postseason, few key pieces remain uncertain.
Shohei Ohtani is on the 15-day injured list with left knee and right biceps issues. He landed there Sept. 11.
Manager Dave Roberts said Monday that Ohtani could begin swinging off a tee as early as this week. The Dodgers expect Ohtani back as a hitter in late September. He won't pitch again this season. Ohtani is batting .277 with 30 home runs and 80 RBIs this year.
Freddie Freeman sat out Monday's game to rest a sore right knee, described as patellar tendinitis. The team does not plan to place him on the injured list. Freeman is expected back in the lineup Tuesday.

“Es difícil decir que alguna vez se sienta rutinario, pero esa es la expectativa aquí. Siempre me río cuando aseguramos un lugar en la postemporada: simplemente hacemos un brindis pequeño y agradable”, dijo el tercera base Max Muncy. “Los muchachos que no han estado aquí ven eso y esperan un poco más. Eso pasa cuando aseguras la división”.
Los bicampeones defensores de la Serie Mundial, que se unieron a Milwaukee y Tampa Bay como equipos que ya aseguraron un lugar en los playoffs, redujeron su número mágico a tres para un quinto título consecutivo del Oeste de la Liga Nacional y el 13ro en 14 temporadas.
Los Ángeles igualó la racha de postemporadas de los Bravos de Atlanta de 1991 a 2005. Los Bravos alcanzaron cinco veces a la Serie Mundial durante ese lapso, pero la única vez que se consagraron fue en 1995.
“Por suerte lo estamos haciendo un poco mejor que eso”, dijo Muncy sobre los tres títulos de los Dodgers y sus cinco participaciones en el Clásico de Otoño durante esta racha.
Tarik Skubal —quien lanzó siete entradas sin permitir carreras y concedió apenas tres hits— señaló que la manera en que los Dodgers manejaron el hecho de asegurar un lugar en la postemporada fue definitivamente distinta en comparación con las situaciones de clasificación que vivió las dos temporadas anteriores con Detroit.
“Creo que eso habla de la gente que está en este vestuario y de lo que esperan de este equipo. Eso estuvo genial. Un pequeño brindis y a seguir. Olvidar que pasó. Tenemos más por lograr esta temporada”, expresó.
Dave Roberts, quien cumple su 11ma temporada como mánager, dijo que su mensaje durante el brindis fue que los Dodgers han logrado mucho hasta este punto, pero aún no se han acercado a jugar su mejor béisbol.
“Cada año pasan muchos jugadores por aquí, y los muchachos encuentran la manera de dar un paso al frente, y eso es de lo que probablemente me siento más orgulloso: la consistencia de ganar a largo plazo. Cualquier equipo, cualquier organización puede ganar en un año determinado cuando las cosas se alinean, pero hacerlo todos los años, cuando se espera que lo hagas, dice algo sobre toda la organización”, dijo Roberts.
Los Dodgers (91-59) actualmente son el segundo sembrado en la Liga Nacional. Están dos juegos y medio por delante de Atlanta y están dos juegos detrás de Milwaukee por el primer puesto.
Un pase directo en la primera ronda es importante en cualquier momento, pero especialmente este año para los Dodgers, que no están a plena capacidad. El primera base Freddie Freeman arrastra molestias en la rodilla derecha y Shohei Ohtani, dos veces Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Nacional, está en la lista de lesionados de 15 días debido a una inflamación en el bíceps derecho.
“Dado cómo están nuestros muchachos en términos de salud, conseguir esa semana sería enorme. Aun así, tenemos que jugar bien para cerrar la temporada y llegar a ese punto”, dijo Roberts antes del juego del lunes.

The two-time reigning World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers are closing in on the National League West title and still have their sights on the NL’s top seed.
Despite the positives, the Dodgers are limping into the opener of a three-game series against the host Cincinnati Reds on Monday.
Los Angeles (90-59) enters play having dropped two straight against the Miami Marlins, including a 6-4 loss on Sunday that saw the club allow four runs in the ninth and a walk-off homer.
Maybe even more concerning is the injury status of manager Dave Roberts’ star players. After placing Shohei Ohtani on the injured list on Friday with knee and biceps ailments, Roberts announced plans to keep first baseman Freddie Freeman out of the lineup on Monday as he deals with right knee tendinitis.
“(Freddie) is obviously not moving as well as he’s used to,” Roberts said. “I’ll give him a chance to recover and then he’ll be back in there on Tuesday. He’s doing everything he can to prepare, but it’s been obvious the last week that he’s not himself in the box.”
Freeman, 37, sat on Wednesday and Friday before returning to the lineup and going 0-for-8 the last two games. The 10-time All-Star is batting .293 with 16 home runs and 66 RBIs this season.
Tarik Skubal (9-7, 2.84 ERA) will make his eighth start since being traded from Detroit to the Dodgers and his second against the Reds in as many appearances. The 29-year-old tossed 7 1/3 innings of two-run, four-hit ball against Cincinnati on Tuesday. The left-hander struck out five and walked two in a 3-2 win.
Skubal has a 2.93 ERA with the Dodgers and has surrendered two earned runs or fewer in four of his last five starts. Still, the two-time American League Cy Young Award winner believes he has more to give. Coming off the longest outing of his short Los Angeles career, Skubal is beginning to live up to his lofty expectations.
“I think that’s ultimately the job of a starting pitcher,” Skubal said of his longest start with the Dodgers on Tuesday. “One, to give your team a chance to win every time you’re out there, and two, to eat as many innings as you can. … I don’t think I’ve thrown the ball as well as I know I’m capable of yet.”
Skubal is 2-0 with a 1.88 ERA in two career starts against the Reds.
With only a few starts left in what’s been a lackluster year, Nick Lodolo (3-4, 5.12) is hoping to correct an inconsistent personal stretch for the Reds (70-79). The 28-year-old has battled through a pair of stints on the injured list due to a blister on his left index finger.
Since returning on Aug. 11, Lodolo has failed to complete five innings in four of six starts. The left-hander faced Skubal and the Dodgers in a losing effort on Tuesday, when he allowed three runs on five hits across 4 2/3 frames. He struck out six and walked three, extending a seven-start stretch without a win.
“I thought early, he wasn’t commanding the ball,” Reds manager Terry Francona said of Lodolo’s last start. “When he got into the third, fourth and fifth (inning), I actually thought he got better. I really wanted him to get through that fifth. I thought it would have been good for him.”
In three career starts against Los Angeles, Lodolo is 0-2 with a 5.52 ERA.
–Field Level Media

By Field Level Media
Sep 15 (Field Level Media) – The Los Angeles Dodgers put relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez on the 15-day injured list due to lower back discomfort on Monday, ending the right-hander’s regular season and causing more upheaval for the team’s bullpen.
Los Angeles has also been nursing Edwin Diaz back in a slow recovery from right elbow surgery with recent Triple-A outings that have not proven successful.
In his most recent appearance for Oklahoma City, Diaz struggled through two- thirds of an inning on Sunday, allowing five runs and three walks in a performance that Dodgers manager Dave Roberts admitted wasn’t going to be enough to merit a promotion.
The Dodgers have left open the possibility for Henriquez to return in the postseason.
Henriquez, 24, has appeared in 61 games (one start) this season, posting a 2.85 ERA with 71 strikeouts against 25 walks in 60 innings.
Diaz, a three-time All-Star, has struggled this season in limited action, logging seven saves in 11 opportunities and an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances.
Los Angeles recalled right-handed pitchers Paul Gervase and Bobby Miller from Triple-A to help shore up their shaky bullpen. Emmet Sheehan was sent to Oklahoma City after throwing six shutout innings in a start against the Miami Marlins on Sunday.
Gervase, 26, has a 2.35 ERA over four major league appearances this season. He owns a lifetime 3.38 ERA with no decisions in 10 outings, all in relief, for the Tampa Bay Rays (2025) and Los Angeles (2025-26).
Miller, 27, has made one big-league appearance in 2026, earning a win over the Washington Nationals on Sept. 6 with three innings of one-run relief. He is 14-8 with a 5.40 ERA in 38 outings (36 starts) for the Dodgers over parts of four seasons.
Sheehan, 26, is 5-8 with a 4.79 ERA in 22 starts this year, 15-12 with a 4.23 ERA in 50 career appearances (45 starts), all with Los Angeles.
(–Field Level Media)

Dodgers might be forced to leave Edwin Díaz off postseason roster
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” from the closer to put him on the playoff roster.
- The Dodgers placed reliever Edgardo Henriquez on the 15-day injured list and recalled Bobby Miller and Paul Gervase.
CINCINNATI — Even as the Dodgers clinched a postseason berth with their 4-1 win over the Reds on Monday, bullpen uncertainty loomed.
When they get to the playoffs, who’s going to take the ball in high-leverage situations?
Their options are dwindling. Edgardo Henriquez landed on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort, ruling him out for the rest of the regular season. Edwin Díaz was so shaky in his rehab assignment Sunday that a spot on the postseason roster isn’t guaranteed.
“We have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff,” manager Dave Roberts said before the Dodgers opened a four-game series against the Reds. “So my bet is that he will be [on the roster]. But there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us to sort of bet on. And so my bet is, yes, but we’ve still got to see something.”
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
Díaz (neck) had the worst outing of his triple-A rehab assignment, surrendering five runs and issuing two walks in two-thirds of an inning. The dud put his return timeline in doubt. His next rehab appearance is scheduled for Wednesday.
“I think the world of him, the baseball card looks great,” Roberts said. “But where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well. So for me, Wednesday, we’ll be watching closely.”
So, who’s still in play?
Tanner Scott remains Roberts’ go-to in save situations. And Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Jack Dreyer and Blake Treinen all have experience in late innings.
On Monday, starter Tarik Skubal gave the group a much-needed break with seven shutout innings. He limited the Reds to three hits and a walk, cruising through their lineup almost three times in 90 pitches.
The Dodgers pulled ahead by four runs, on home runs from Kyle Tucker and Teoscar Hernández, who have both broken out of slumps, and an RBI single from Kiké Hernández.
With the game still relatively tight, Vesia entered in the bottom of the eighth to face the left-handed heavy bottom of the order. He retired the side.
Phillips and Treinen both were warming in the ninth when the Dodgers got a runner to second base with one out. When they failed to score him, Phillips jogged in to face the top of the order. He surrendered a high-flying solo homer to Elly De La Cruz on a fastball above the zone but avoided further damage.
Before the game, the Dodgers added two fresh arms to the bullpen. They recalled right-handers Bobby Miller and Paul Gervase, as they put Henriquez on the IL and optioned right-hander Emmet Sheehan.
Henriquez will undergo imaging on the area, which Roberts said stretched to his side near his oblique.
“The hope is we’ll get him back in the postseason,” Roberts said.
Roberts said he didn’t know what the move meant for Sheehan, who in his past two starts limited opponents to one run and recorded 15 strikeouts in a combined 11 ⅔ innings.
“Some of it’s probably contingent on Roki [Sasaki], and we’ve got another start coming up down the road here, as far as a bullpen kind of situation,” Roberts said. “So I don’t know, but Emmet’s done everything he can do in his power to force our hand, which I love. The last two have been really good.”
Sasaki (right middle finger blister) could start Thursday. His bullpen session Monday marked the first time he had tested covering the sensitive area on his finger with Dermabond, Roberts said.
“We just can’t put him in a position to go backward,” Roberts said.
The Dodgers also have more bullpen reinforcements coming.
Another bullpen addition is left-hander Kris Bubic, who met the team in Cincinnati and is in place to make his Dodgers debut later this week. Bubic made his last rehab appearance for triple-A Oklahoma City on Sunday, so Roberts said the Dodgers likely won’t activate him off the 60-day injured list until Wednesday at the earliest.
The Dodgers acquired Bubic from the Kansas City Royals at the trade deadline this year. He’d been on the IL since May, first with a low-grade flexor strain in his left forearm, and then a shoulder impingement setback.
In six triple-A rehab appearances over 5⅔ innings, Bubic didn’t yield a run and he limited opponents to two hits and two walks.
Roberts was noncommittal about Bubic being a high-leverage option.
“Seems like all of our games are leverage these days,” he said.
By not putting Shohei Ohtani on the injured list in July or in August, the Dodgers may have compromised the two-way star’s ability to be healthy for the playoffs.

Claves: La rodilla de Freeman, el bate de Ohtani y el cálculo de octubre de Dodgers
CINCINNATI — Freddie Freeman no estuvo en la alineación de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles para el juego del lunes por la noche contra los Rojos de Cincinnati mientras lidia con molestias en la rodilla derecha.
Aunque el primera base no ha estado en la alineación en tres de los últimos cinco juegos, el mánager Dave Roberts manifestó que poner a Freeman en la lista de lesionados de 10 días para dejarlo listo para la postemporada —algo similar a lo que hicieron con Shohei Ohtani— no es una opción en este momento.
“No creo que (el descanso) tenga que ser de 10 días, pero ¿podría ser más de uno? Esa es una pregunta válida. Tengo que hablar un poco con el cuerpo de preparadores, con Freddie, y al final tomar esa decisión. Pero no creo que la lista de lesionados tenga sentido”, comentó Roberts.
Roberts señaló que no creía que Freeman fuera a tener problemas persistentes con la rodilla durante la postemporada si se puede manejar adecuadamente. Freeman batea para .293, pero está de 3 en sus últimos 30 turnos, con nueve ponches.
Los campeones defensores de la Serie Mundial por segundo año consecutivo llegaron al lunes por la noche con un número mágico de cuatro para asegurar su 13er título del Oeste de la Liga Nacional en 14 años. Su mayor preocupación es asegurarse de amarrar uno de los dos primeros puestos de preclasificación y un pase directo en la primera ronda.
Los Dodgers (90-59) llegaron al lunes con una ventaja de 2 1/2 juegos sobre Atlanta por el segundo puesto. Milwaukee (93-57) tiene la mejor marca de la Liga Nacional.
“Dado cómo están nuestros muchachos en cuanto a salud, conseguir esa semana sería enorme. Aun así, tenemos que jugar bien para cerrar la temporada y llegar a ese punto”, expresó Roberts.
Ohtani, quien ha estado en la lista de lesionados de 15 días desde el 8 de septiembre debido a una inflamación en el bíceps derecho, hará swings desde un tee en Los Ángeles el martes. Serán sus primeros swings desde que ingresó a la lista de lesionados. Roberts indicó que Ohtani ha estado levantando pesas, entrenando y recibiendo tratamiento en los últimos días.
Con Ohtani fuera del viaje de siete juegos, definitivamente ha habido un ambiente distinto en el clubhouse.
“Se siente diferente porque él tiene mucha presencia cuando está en el campo. La última serie no fue indicativa, pero creo que en general estamos jugando buen béisbol. Sabemos que somos mejores con Shohei. Probablemente los aficionados estén decepcionados, pero no creo que nosotros realmente lo hayamos sentido”, dijo Roberts.
La mayor preocupación podría estar con el relevista Edwin Díaz, quien ha permitido seis carreras limpias en 3 1/3 entradas en cuatro apariciones de rehabilitación con Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Díaz no solo está lidiando con una inflamación en el cuello, sino también con problemas de control. Díaz firmó un contrato de 59 millones de dólares por tres años durante la temporada baja y ha tenido dificultades en su primer año en Los Ángeles.
El derecho tendrá otra salida el miércoles, pero Roberts sí dejó abierta la posibilidad de que Díaz quede fuera de los rosters de postemporada.
“Necesita lanzar mejor. No ha sido bueno. La tarjeta de béisbol se ve genial. Pero, tal como estamos, tiene que haber algo a lo que podamos aferrarnos. Y él lo sabe. Quiere lanzar bien”, afirmó Roberts.
